papers.abstract_full: Folate deficiency is associated with increased risk of conotruncal heart defects (CTHD), but its interaction with genetic factors remains unclear. Our objective was to investigate genome-wide associations between common genetic variants and birth before versus after universal folic acid fortification among children with CTHD and other heart defects. Sequencing data were available through the Pediatric Cardiac Genomics Consortium, aligned to the human reference genome (GRCh38/hg38), and jointly processed to ensure uniform variant detection and minimize batch effects. Analyses were restricted to individuals with European-inferred genetic ancestry, limiting generalizability to other ancestral groups. Genome-wide association study (GWAS) models compared allele frequencies across fortification eras among all participants (n = 1285), the subset with CTHD (n = 534), and the remaining individuals with other heart defects (n = 751). Functional enrichment was assessed using the Database for Annotation, Visualization and Integrated Discovery (DAVID). Among the full analytic group, eight loci had at least two suggestive variants before compared to after fortification. Among the subset with CTHD, two variants located in DHRS3 (rs7551703, odds ratio [OR] 2.10, and rs6541043, OR 2.21) and four variants located in PPARGC1B showed suggestive association after fortification (OR 4.47-4.51). Enriched biological pathway terms were consistent with cardiac developmental processes. In summary, this study examined the association between folic acid fortification and genetic risk for CTHD and other heart defects and identified associations with fortification era that suggest some shift in risk following fortification. Identified pathways suggest gene-nutrient interactions may modulate cardiac developmental pathways, underscoring the relationship between maternal folate status and cardiovascular development.

papers.title: hvantk: an agentic multi-omics framework for variant annotation and analysis
papers.abstract: Large-scale genetic variant analysis involves multiple computational steps, data formats, gene and variant annotation sources and compute requirements. Some of the steps like joint calling for large cohorts are run on large compute clusters, while gene/variant classification algorithms can be run in a desktop computer. At the same time, variant annotations such as gene expression and gene constraints metrics from gnomAD are provided in different formats, by resources that frequently change their…
papers.abstract_full: Large-scale genetic variant analysis involves multiple computational steps, data formats, gene and variant annotation sources and compute requirements. Some of the steps like joint calling for large cohorts are run on large compute clusters, while gene/variant classification algorithms can be run in a desktop computer. At the same time, variant annotations such as gene expression and gene constraints metrics from gnomAD are provided in different formats, by resources that frequently change their versions. Here, we present  hvantk , a framework that provides a common data model for large-scale annotation and analysis of genetic variants, by extending popular data formats such as Hail MatrixTable and AnnData. hvantk agentically integrates 21 public multi-omic data providers as plugins that a developer, bioinformatician or an AI agent can author without modifying the framework’s core, drives analysis workflows using agent skills, and scales from single desktop computers to high-performance computing clusters. We used hvantk for reanalysing three case-control cohorts, comprising congenital heart disease (CHD), developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (Epi25) and schizophrenia (SCHEMA). Re-ranking of gene-based burden testing results using multi-omic annotations improved the recovery of curated disease genes from 26% to 49% in CHD, 40% to 48% in Epi25 and 51% to 54% in SCHEMA, among the top decile re-ranked genes. Expression at bulk and single-cell levels were the features contributing the most over a baseline of burden, gene constraint and publication count.

papers.abstract_full: Background  Hypoplastic Left Heart Syndrome (HLHS) is a severe congenital heart defect characterized by underdevelopment of left-sided cardiac structures, requiring staged surgical palliation that establishes the right ventricle as the single ventricle maintaining systemic circulation. After surgery, patients remain highly susceptible to heart failure, possibly due to the increased hemodynamic load imposed on the single surviving ventricle. Because the etiology of HLHS remains poorly understood, elucidating the mechanisms that drive ventricular dysfunction requires model systems that capture both patient-specific genetics and the dynamic mechanical environment of the ventricle. Thus, our objective was to compare how induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived cardiomyocytes (iPSC-CMs) from patients with HLHS differ from control in static culture and in response to cyclic stretch. Methods  Control iPSCs from two unaffected donors and iPSCs from four HLHS patients were differentiated into iPSC-CMs, engineered into aligned tissues, and cultured statically or exposed to cyclic 20% uniaxial stretch at 1 Hz for 48h. Sarcomere organization was quantified in static tissues using images of immunostained α-actinin. Calcium transients at 1 Hz pacing frequency in static and stretched tissues were evaluated using Fluo-4 calcium indicator dye. Bulk RNA sequencing was performed to evaluate stretch-induced transcriptomic changes in control and HLHS iPSC-CMs. Results  In static culture, HLHS iPSC-CMs had modest defects in sarcomere organization and calcium transient morphology compared to control. In response to cyclic stretch, control iPSC-CMs exhibited calcium transients with quicker rise time, a response observed in only one of four lines of HLHS iPSC-CMs. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that all four lines of HLHS iPSC-CMs failed to upregulate calcium handling and sarcomere-associated genes in response to stretch, unlike control iPSC-CMs. Stretch also induced HLHS iPSC-CMs to exhibit pronounced activation of inflammatory signaling pathways, a response not observed in control iPSC-CMs. Conclusions  iPSC-CMs from HLHS patients demonstrate aberrant responses to cyclic stretch, including blunted adaptation of calcium transients and heightened inflammatory signaling. These findings implicate defective mechanoadaptation as a potential contributor to single ventricle failure and identify potential candidate biomarkers and new opportunities for therapeutic interventions for HLHS patients.

papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: Mental disorders and heart failure frequently co-occur, but their shared genetic architecture remains incompletely understood. METHODS: Prospective Cox regression analysis in the UK Biobank (UKB) quantified the risk of incident heart failure associated with mental disorders. Linkage disequilibrium score regression estimated genetic correlations, while multitrait genome-wide association and cross-phenotype association analyses identified candidate pleiotropic loci. Statistical fine mapping and gene-level association analyses prioritized candidate variants and genes. Bayesian colocalization assessed evidence for shared candidate variants, and exploratory Gene Ontology biological-process overrepresentation analysis provided descriptive biological context. Single-cell RNA sequencing and genetically informed spatial mapping (gsMap) provided cellular and spatial context for prioritized genes. Geneformer-based in silico perturbation analysis was performed using a cardiac cell atlas of dilated cardiomyopathy to prioritize candidate pleiotropic genes and identify cardiac cell states showing predicted embedding shifts. RESULTS: Prospective UKB analyses demonstrated that mental disorders, such as posttraumatic stress disorder, depression, and bipolar disorder, were associated with a higher risk of incident heart failure. Multitrait analysis identified 607 pleiotropic variants, with fine-mapping and colocalization converging on prioritized candidate loci, including TMEM18, NKX2-2, and XRN2. Single-cell expression profiling and spatial mapping provided context at the cellular and tissue levels for the prioritized genes. Geneformer-based in silico perturbation prioritized FOXP1 and TMEM106B as leading pleiotropic candidate genes on the basis of their predicted changes in downstream gene embeddings in cardiac cellular contexts. CONCLUSIONS: This study identifies shared genetic architecture between mental disorders and heart failure and prioritizes candidate pleiotropic genes associated with both. Transcriptomic and in silico perturbation analyses provide exploratory cellular, spatial, and cardiac functional context. Functional validation is required before mechanistic or therapeutic interpretation.

papers.abstract_full: PURPOSE OF REVIEW: This review aims to evaluate the contemporary and evolving role of cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging in arrhythmic risk stratification for patients with non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy, specifically focussing on dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) and non-dilated left ventricular cardiomyopathy (NDLVC). This review synthesises current data on late gadolinium enhancement (LGE), parametric mapping, strain imaging and artificial intelligence (AI), and contextualises these among emerging genetic risk stratification approaches. RECENT FINDINGS: Left ventricular ejection fraction has been the cornerstone for guideline-based arrhythmic risk stratification in patients with DCM, despite limited precision. Observational data and meta-analyses have established the presence of replacement fibrosis through LGE-CMR as a powerful independent predictor of ventricular arrhythmias (VAs) and sudden cardiac death. Crucially, the absence of LGE identifies a low-risk cohort. Much recent focus has been on understanding whether more precise characterisation of scar can further enhance arrhythmic risk stratification, for example through scar quantification. Although data exists supporting a potential role for T1 mapping for arrhythmic risk prediction in this cohort, further research is required to support its widespread adoption. Emerging multimodal approaches using artificial intelligence and personalised computational "digital twins" are areas of important interest, offering scope for integration of imaging, electrocardiographic and genomic data layers. Arrhythmic risk stratification in non-ischaemic cardiomyopathies remains challenging despite significant advances. Progressive refinement in precision has accompanied a shift from a restrictive, functional assessment towards an integrated, substrate-driven precision model. CMR represents the cornerstone of this evolution.

papers.abstract_full: IMPORTANCE: Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) is a major cause of heart failure that disproportionately affects individuals of predominantly African ancestry, among whom familial clustering of disease is more pronounced relative to those of predominantly European ancestry. Truncating variants in TTN, which encodes the sarcomeric protein titin, are the most common established monogenic cause of DCM. A common CD36 nonsense variant enriched among individuals of African ancestry has also been shown to account for a substantial burden of DCM. OBJECTIVE: To compare the contribution of a CD36 nonsense variant to DCM risk with that of truncating variants in TTN and pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in other established genes for DCM. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: Multicohort genetic association study including participants of African and European ancestry with exome or genome sequence data and DCM case status from the following 4 US datasets: All of Us Research Program (recruitment: 2017-present; last follow-up: August 27, 2024), Million Veteran Program (recruitment: 2011-present; last follow-up: September 30, 2024), Penn Medicine Biobank (recruitment: 2013-present; last follow-up: November 14, 2022), and the DCM Precision Medicine Study (recruitment: 2016-2020; last follow-up: March 15, 2020). EXPOSURE: Carrier status for TTN truncating variants, pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in 11 high-confidence genes for DCM, and the nonsense variant CD36 Y325* (0, 1, or 2 copies). MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Risk of DCM, prevalence of variant carriers among DCM cases, and population attributable fraction of DCM. RESULTS: Among 82 623 individuals of predominantly African ancestry across 4 cohorts, the mean age was 53.4 years (SD, 13.9 years), 47 124 were male, and 1316 had DCM. Individuals who were homozygous for the CD36 Y325* risk allele had a higher risk of DCM (odds ratio [OR], 4.8; 95% CI, 3.1-7.3) as did those who were heterozygous (OR, 1.4; 95% CI, 1.2-1.7). TTN truncating variants also conferred an elevated risk of DCM in participants of African ancestry (OR, 8.5; 95% CI, 5.5-13.0). Among 1316 individuals of African ancestry classified as DCM cases, 33 (2.5%) were homozygous for CD36, 56 (4.3%) had TTN truncating variants, and 16 (1.2%) had pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in other high-confidence genes for DCM. In population-level analyses incorporating both heterozygous and homozygous CD36 Y325* carriers, the population attributable fraction for CD36 (9.0% [6.2% for heterozygous carriers and 2.8% for homozygous carriers]) surpassed the population attributable fraction for TTN truncating variants (3.7%). CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In 4 US cohorts, an ancestry-specific CD36 variant contributed more to DCM burden among individuals of African ancestry than established genes for DCM, including TTN truncating variants that are typically considered the most common genetic cause. These findings reshape the known genetic architecture of DCM in individuals of African ancestry and highlight the importance of representation in genomic research.

papers.abstract_full: OBJECTIVE: To identify factors associated with predischarge morbidity and mortality among small for gestational age infants. STUDY DESIGN: We conducted a retrospective single-center cohort study of small for gestational age infants admitted to a level IV neonatal intensive care unit. We determined the association of clinical characteristics, congenital anomalies, and genetic disorders with the primary outcome of predischarge morbidity or mortality and characterized morbidity and mortality across congenital anomaly subgroups. RESULTS: Among 293 small for gestational age infants, 18 (6.1%) had a genetic disorder and 103 (35.2%) had a major congenital anomaly, with congenital heart disease (CHD) representing the largest subgroup. The primary outcome of morbidity or mortality occurred in 93 infants (31.7%); 74 infants (25.3%) experienced morbidity and 19 (6.5%) died. CHD (adjusted odds ratio [aOR]: 16.5, 95% CI 6.44-45.7) and multiple congenital anomalies (aOR: 17.8, 95% CI 4.64-71.1) were found to be strongly associated with morbidity or mortality, after accounting for sex, maternal race, and intubation > 7 days. Statistically significant associations were also found with the presence of musculoskeletal anomalies as well as genetic disorders in infants without congenital anomalies, though in limited sample sizes. CHD was the largest contributor to morbidity, whereas multiple congenital anomalies accounted for the greatest proportion of mortality. Infants with abdominal wall defects and central nervous system anomalies experienced no morbidity or mortality. CONCLUSION: Congenital heart disease and multiple congenital anomalies were strongly associated with morbidity and mortality among SGA infants, whereas the degree of SGA alone was not. These findings suggest that risk is not explained by the degree of SGA alone and may be more strongly associated with congenital disease and other underlying factors. KEY POINTS: Risk is highly variable in SGA infantsCHD predicts adverse outcomesMultiple anomalies predict adverse outcomesDegree of SGA alone does not explain risk.

papers.abstract_full: During development, collective and oriented cell behaviors that drive organ formation and tissue patterning require coordination among neighboring cells governed by the highly conserved planar cell polarity (PCP) pathway. Deficiencies in PCP gene function result in severe developmental defects in model systems from flies to mice, while PCP gene mutations are associated with human birth defects impacting the neural tube and heart. Atypical cadherin Celsr1 engages in cell-cell adhesion to coordinate the asymmetric localization of Fz6 and Vangl2 to opposing sides of the PCP junction between neighboring cells. However, whether CELSR1 genetic variations disrupt function or contribute to disease pathogenesis remains poorly understood. Using cell-based assays for Celsr1 function, along with in silico modeling, we test a cohort of 17 Celsr1 mutations previously identified in patients with neural tube and congenital heart defects. In junctional enrichment assays, we find 13 variants displayed altered enrichment at cell borders relative to WT, including both loss- and gain-of-function behaviors. Further analysis of select Celsr1 mutations revealed defects in membrane mobility and perturbed co-recruitment of PCP protein Fz6. Our findings link Celsr1 mutations associated with human birth defects to functional defects in adhesion and PCP. In addition, our approach supports a framework for evaluating PCP function alongside genomics and in silico predictions toward understanding the pathophysiology impacts of genetic variations associated with human developmental disorders and gaining insight into Celsr1 function during development.

papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Kleefstra syndrome type 1 (KLEFS1) is a rare neurodevelopmental disorder caused by pathogenic variants in EHMT1, which play a key role in epigenetic regulation. Core features include global developmental delay (GDD), intellectual disability (ID), facial dysmorphism, congenital heart defects (CHDs), and neuropsychiatric manifestations. METHODS: This retrospective study included patients with KLEFS1 evaluated at Seoul National University Hospital between January 2022 and April 2025. Genetic diagnoses were made using chromosomal microarray or whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing, and clinical data were extracted from medical records. To enhance statistical power, we conducted a joint analysis with established cohorts of at least 30 clinically characterized patients. RESULTS: Among the 15 patients with KLEFS1, 14 (93.3%) exhibited GDD or ID, with frequent comorbidities such as CHDs (8/12, 66.7%), orthopaedic manifestations (6/12, 50.0%), epilepsy (6/15, 40.0%), and sleep problems (4/11, 36.4%). Brain MRI revealed abnormalities in 10 of the 12 patients (83.3%), including pituitary anomalies in 2 (16.7%). By combining our data with recently published multicenter international cohorts, we assessed genotype-phenotype correlations by comparing the clinical features of 202 patients with different variant subtypes. Patients with multigene deletions had a significantly higher prevalence of CHDs (53.5% vs 25.8%, p value = 2 × 10-4), cortical visual impairment (12.5% vs 1.7%, p value = 0.004), microcephaly (37.1% vs 17.8%, p value = 0.009), corpus callosum abnormalities (17.9% vs 5.9%, p value = 0.02), and hearing impairment (39.7% vs 25.6%, p value = 0.04) than those with single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) or short insertions/deletions (indels), in addition to the previously identified features including epilepsy, constipation, and short stature. We also observed that a recurrent EHMT1 variant (p.Arg948Trp), identified in multiple unrelated patients, was linked to significant phenotypic heterogeneity, including late-onset neurocognitive regression. DISCUSSION: Our study showed that patients with multigene deletions are significantly more likely to exhibit multiorgan involvement, including CHDs, cortical visual impairments, microcephaly, corpus callosum abnormalities, and hearing impairments, compared with those with SNVs or indels, emphasizing the importance of genotype-informed management. We report pituitary gland abnormalities in KLEFS1, expanding the phenotypic and neuroimaging spectrum of KLEFS1. The patient showing regression in their 30s necessitates long-term, comprehensive studies to support care.

papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: Cardiomyopathy with a restrictive phenotype is uncommon, genetically heterogeneous, and difficult to distinguish from advanced hypertrophic or dilated cardiomyopathy. We aimed primarily to determine the diagnostic yield and spectrum of pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants among patients with an echocardiographically defined restrictive phenotype; genotype-imaging and survival comparisons were prespecified exploratory analyses. METHODS: We screened 568 patients with cardiomyopathy who underwent whole-exome sequencing and comprehensive echocardiography. Thirty-three met the operational definition of restrictive phenotype. Variants were classified. Genotype-imaging associations and survival were analyzed exploratorily. RESULTS: Among the 568 patients, 33 exhibited a restrictive phenotype: 7 had restrictive cardiomyopathy (RCM), 20 had hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with a restrictive phenotype (HRCM), and 6 had dilated cardiomyopathy with a restrictive phenotype (HDRCM). Variant carriers had a smaller aortic sinus diameter. In addition, MYBPC3 variant carriers had greater ventricular wall thickness and more frequent septal hypertrophy. Both the HRCM and HDRCM groups showed hypertrophic features, with interventricular septal hypertrophy occurring more frequently in the HDRCM group. The estimated 5-year survival was 54.5%, and survival did not differ significantly according to genetic-variant status. CONCLUSIONS: Pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants were frequent in this single-center cohort with restrictive physiology and were associated with selected imaging features. These exploratory findings support integrated genetic and echocardiographic evaluation.

papers.abstract_full: Truncating variants in the TTN gene (TTNtv) are the most common genetic causes of dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM). Despite this high prevalence, the clinical spectrum of TTNtv-associated cardiomyopathy remains incompletely characterized, with variable penetrance, expressivity, and phenotypic manifestations. In this study, we present four cases of TTNtv cardiomyopathy illustrating diverse clinical presentations: an asymptomatic phenotype with moderate left ventricular systolic dysfunction discovered through screening, a severe arrhythmic phenotype with ventricular tachycardia storm requiring multiple ablations and implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) shocks, a recurrent stress-induced (takotsubo) presentation with two discrete episodes, which we present as a hypothesis-generating observation, and an inflammatory presentation with fluorodeoxyglucose-positron emission tomography (FDG-PET) evidence of active myocardial inflammation and symptomatic response to corticosteroids. These cases illustrate the potential clinical value of genetic testing, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, and individualized assessment in TTNtv cardiomyopathy, and suggest that genetic counseling and cascade testing should be considered for affected individuals and their families.

papers.abstract_full: Mutations in β-cardiac myosin are a common cause of inherited cardiomyopathies. The dilated cardiomyopathy E525K mutation alters both thick filament regulation and motor activity, yet the structural basis for these effects has remained unclear. Here, we combined cryo-EM and MD simulations to determine how E525K affects the conformational landscape of cardiac myosin in both its autoinhibited interacting-heads motif (IHM) and isolated myosin head states. E525K-mutated myosin exclusively adopted a single S2 conformation in IHM, in contrast to the conformational heterogeneity observed in wild-type myosin. Structural and electrostatic analyses revealed that the mutation increased positive charge density at the blocked-head (BH) - S2 (subfragment-2) interface, strengthening interactions with negatively charged residues within S2. 3D variability analysis and MD simulations of the E525K IHM demonstrated reduced S2 mobility, consistent with strengthened BH - S2 interactions, and decreased conformational flexibility, providing a structural mechanism for stabilization of the IHM state. To investigate the isolated myosin head, we determined cryo-EM structures of wild-type and E525K subfragment-1 (S1). The mutation induced local conformational rearrangements in the activation-loop and Loop 3 region, the SH3-like domain, and the essential light chain of S1, revealing structural changes that support the enhanced motor activity previously reported for isolated E525K myosin motors. These findings show that E525K stabilizes the autoinhibited IHM through electrostatic stabilization of the BH - S2 interface while inducing structural changes consistent with activation of the isolated motor domain, providing structural insights into how a single DCM mutation differentially regulates cardiac myosin S1 and IHM structure and function.

papers.abstract_full: PURPOSE: Pathogenic variants in CDH2 cause agenesis of the corpus callosum, cardiac, ocular, and genital syndrome (ACOGS). We aimed to define the clinical and molecular landscape of CDH2-related developmental disorders. METHODS: Newly identified and previously reported families were analyzed for genotype-phenotype correlations; variants were assessed using protein modeling and splicing assays. RESULTS: Screening identified 20 new families carrying (likely) pathogenic ((L)P) alleles (n=16) or high-priority variants of uncertain significance (VUS) (n=4), including 12 novel CDH2 alleles. The combined (L)P cohort (37 individuals) showed variable ACOGS core features (mean 3; range 1-5), along with abdominal wall and/or diaphragmatic hernias and nipple, spine or gastrointestinal anomalies, each seen in ∼20% of individuals. Novel ACOGS findings included ambiguous genitalia, female genital malformations and dilated cardiomyopathy. Missense variants, principally within extracellular cadherin domains, accounted for 86% of unique (L)P alleles with clusters in EC1 and EC4-EC5; the remainder produce late protein truncations or in-frame deletions. Disruption of calcium binding was predicted by modeling. Conversely, VUS were primarily nonsense-mediated decay-sensitive or deletions (71%), linked to neurodevelopmental, kidney or other anomalies. CONCLUSION: We expand the ACOGS spectrum and highlight its striking clinical variability. Additionally, we identify a possible milder phenotype associated with CDH2 haploinsufficiency.

papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: gCMP are a major cause of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. While agonistic anti-β1-adrenergic receptor antibodies (anti-β1AR-ECII) have a recognized pathogenic role in idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM), the relevance of HRA in gCMP remains unclear. METHODS: One hundred gCMP patients with confirmed genetic variants in cardiomyopathy genes were compared with 100 age- and sex-matched healthy individuals. Antibody reactivities were quantified using bead-based flow cytometric assays against cardiac antigens: The second extracellular loop of the β1 adrenergic receptor (β1AR-ECII), Troponin I3 (TPI3), Tropomyosin 1 (TPM1), Myosin heavy chain 6 and 7 (MYH6, MYH7) and Myosin light chain 7 (MYL7). RESULTS: gCMP patients showed higher anti-TPI3 and lower anti-TPM1 antibody levels compared to controls indicating increased induction of the former and loss of the latter in gCMP patients. Age and sex influenced HRA patterns in both groups. Anti-MYH6 and anti-TPM1 antibody levels were negatively associated with left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), both overall and within specific gCMP subtypes, including hypertrophic and arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy. Additionally, anti-MYH6 antibody levels were negatively associated with right ventricular function, measured by tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (TAPSE). CONCLUSION: Our findings stress the diagnostic potential of HRA profiling and indicate that gCMP patients might profit from therapeutic targeting of HRA.

papers.abstract_full: Background and Clinical Significance: Cardiofaciocutaneous syndrome (CFC) is a rare autosomal dominant RASopathy characterized by craniofacial dysmorphism, congenital heart defects, cutaneous abnormalities, growth impairment, and neurodevelopmental delay. Pathogenic variants in KRAS account for a minority of cases and define cardiofaciocutaneous syndrome type 2 (CFC2). Establishing a molecular diagnosis is often challenging because of the substantial clinical overlap among RASopathies, including Noonan and Costello syndromes. Case Presentation: We describe a one-year-old boy presenting with macrocephaly, ventriculomegaly, hypotonia, developmental delay, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, gastroesophageal reflux, and mild dermatological abnormalities. To clarify the diagnosis, a custom next-generation sequencing panel targeting RASopathy-associated genes was performed. Genetic analysis identified a heterozygous KRAS variant, NM_033360.4:c.101C>G, p.(Pro34Arg), which was confirmed by Sanger sequencing and shown to have arisen de novo through parental testing. Additional variants of uncertain significance were detected in ABCC9, CACNA1G, and DES; however, these were considered unlikely to account for the phenotype because of limited clinical concordance and current ACMG/AMP classification. The KRAS variant was classified as pathogenic based on its de novo occurrence, absence from population databases, localization within a critical functional domain, supportive computational evidence, and previously reported pathogenic substitutions affecting the same residue. Conclusions: This case provides additional evidence supporting the pathogenicity of KRAS p.(Pro34Arg), a variant reported only rarely in association with CFC. The observed phenotype further expands the clinical spectrum of KRAS-associated CFC and highlights the value of comprehensive molecular testing for the differential diagnosis of RASopathies and the refinement of genotype-phenotype correlations.

papers.abstract_full: Newborn screening (NBS) is an essential public health intervention for early detection and secondary prevention of inherited disorders in asymptomatic infants at birth. Advances in this field and the accessibility of new screening methods and therapies in the last decade have insurmountably surpassed Malaysia's national NBS programme, which has stagnated. Currently, our mandatory nationwide routine screening is limited to only two conditions: glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency and congenital hypothyroidism. While services such as universal newborn hearing and critical congenital heart disease screening are available in many settings, most treatable genetic and metabolic disorders remain unscreened. Consequently, preventable morbidity and mortality, from inborn errors of immunity and metabolism, and genetic diseases persist. This position statement reviews the evidence for expanding the national NBS programme in Malaysia, arguing that a modernised, contemporary and pragmatic method is both clinically tenable and morally imperative. By embracing advancements for expanded NBS, Malaysia can safeguard children's right to an open future, fulfil intergenerational justice, and ensure that no infant is left without the opportunity for life-saving care.

papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: Trisomy 21 is associated with combined immune dysregulation, including lymphopenia, impaired responses to vaccines, and heightened susceptibility to respiratory infections, driven in part by triplication of chromosome 21-encoded interferon receptor genes. BACH2 haploinsufficiency is a rare monogenic immunodeficiency characterized by lymphopenia, hypogammaglobulinemia, and susceptibility to infections and autoimmune diseases. Co-occurrence of these two conditions has not been previously described. CASE PRESENTATION: We report a 5-year longitudinal course in a Kenyan girl with trisomy 21, congenital heart disease, aspiration, and severe gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) found via whole exome sequencing to carry a heterozygous BACH2 missense variant (c.1420C > G;p.Leu474Val) of uncertain significance; parental segregation remains incomplete. In silico protein structural modeling (FoldX and Missense3D) yielded discordant predictions of the variant's effect on the protein's stability and structure. Additional in silico pathogenicity predictions were also inconsistent: Sorting Intolerant from Tolerant (SIFT), Evolutionary Model of Variant Effect (EVE), PolyPhen-2, and CADD Phred scores predicted pathogenicity, while REVEL and AlphaMissense suggested a lack of deleteriousness. Persistent panlymphopenia and profoundly low IgM levels were documented throughout the follow-up period. Over these 5 years, the girl sustained six hospitalized lower respiratory tract infections (LRTIs), with four requiring intensive care, which were disseminated Bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) disease, respiratory syncytial virus and SARS-CoV-2 infections, and influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 pneumonia. Chest computed tomography at 4 years showed bilateral consolidations without bronchiectasis. Annual autoimmune screening remained negative. CONCLUSION: This case illustrates the burden caused by severe and diverse respiratory pathogenic infections in a child with trisomy 21 and a candidate BACH2 variant. Trisomy 21 alone plausibly explains much of the phenotype; an independent contribution from the BACH2 variant remains unproven pending functional and segregation studies. Clinical considerations supported by this case include the potential value of prevaccination immunological screening to prevent BCG disease, equitable access to viral prophylaxis, and early specialist engagement in refractory cases.

papers.abstract_full: Abstract  Alagille Syndrome is a rare, autosomal dominant, multisystem disorder, mainly associated with mutations in the JAG1 gene and, to a lesser extent, NOTCH2. It is associated with bile duct paucity and a spectrum of cholestasis, congenital heart defects (especially peripheral pulmonary stenosis), skeletal defects, ocular defects (posterior embryotoxon), renal defects, and characteristic facial features. Clinical presentation is highly variable, even within the same family carrying identical genetic mutations, which complicates diagnosis and treatment. Progress in molecular genetics, particularly regarding the Notch signalling pathway, has enhanced diagnostic accuracy and clarified disease pathogenesis. Hepatic manifestations, usually presenting in infancy, may progress to end-stage liver disease requiring transplantation. Cardiac and vascular anomalies are significant contributors to poor survival and represent a special management concern. A common and complex presentation includes neuropsychological delay, growth failure, and nutritional deficiencies, all of which require management by a multidisciplinary team. In atypical or mild cases, genetic testing has emerged as an important diagnostic tool. Management focuses on symptom control, nutritional support, and organ-specific interventions, and new drugs targeting bile acid metabolism and the Notch pathway show promise. This review provides a thorough overview of Alagille Syndrome, highlighting its clinical heterogeneity, underlying genetic mechanisms, diagnostic dilemmas, and evolving therapeutic approaches.

papers.abstract_full: Preventing sudden cardiac death (SCD) in early non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy (NICM) remains a major clinical challenge. Traditional risk stratification centred on left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) poorly captures arrhythmic risk, particularly in early dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) and non-dilated left ventricular cardiomyopathy (NDLVC). Increasing recognition of fibrosis-based and genotype-specific arrhythmogenic substrates has prompted a shift towards multimodal risk assessment strategies integrating imaging, electrocardiographic, and genetic data. This review examines contemporary approaches to risk stratification in early NICM, with particular emphasis on the role of cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging and late gadolinium enhancement (LGE). The expanding role of genotype-specific phenotyping is also explored, including high-risk arrhythmogenic variants and the integration of genotype with imaging phenotype as a promising route to improved prediction. Collectively, these advances support a transition from population-based LVEF thresholds towards more personalised and biologically informed strategies for prevention of SCD in early NICM.

papers.abstract_full: Kartagener's syndrome (KS) is a rare, typically autosomal recessive ciliopathy and a subtype of primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD), characterized by situs inversus, bronchiectasis, and chronic sinusitis. KS accounts for approximately 50% of PCD cases and results from impaired motile cilia function. Defective embryonic nodal ciliary beating leads to stochastic left-right axis determination and situs abnormalities. Although numerous genes have been implicated in PCD, up to 30% of cases remain genetically unresolved, and studies specifically focused on KS cohorts remain limited. Here, we performed whole exome sequencing in 17 adult patients from a Turkish KS cohort to identify pathogenic variants and novel candidate genes. Variants were prioritised based on sequencing quality, population allele frequency, and predicted functional impact, and included single-nucleotide variants, small insertions/deletions, and copy-number variations. The restriction of the cohort to individuals with situs inversus provided a phenotype-specific context for variant interpretation, as genes not typically associated with left-right axis determination were less likely to account for disease in this study population. Pathogenic or potentially disease-associated variants were identified in multiple established PCD genes, including DNAH5, DNAI1, DNAI2, DNAAF1, DNAAF3, CFAP300, and ODAD1, with several novel alleles detected. In one patient lacking biallelic variants in known PCD genes, expanded analysis identified heterozygous variants in the cilia-associated genes DLEC1 and DNAAF9 together with a hemizygous copy number loss in EZR, a gene known to affect motile cilia function. The possible relevance of these concurrent findings warrants further investigation in genetically unresolved cases. Overall, analysis of this KS-specific cohort demonstrated a high diagnostic yield, expanded the variant spectrum associated with Kartagener's syndrome, and further supported the utility of phenotype-driven genomic analysis in genetically heterogeneous ciliopathies.

papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND AND AIM: Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia (PCD) is a genetic disorder characterized by respiratory infections leading to chronic airway colonization and progressive lung damage. The aim of this study is to evaluate prevalence and longitudinal changes of respiratory microbiological profile in children and young adults with PCD, and their association with clinical, functional, and radiological features. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This prospective, multicenter longitudinal study included PCD patients from seven Italian Pediatric Pulmonology centers within the SIMRI (Italian Pediatric Respiratory Society) "PCD and Non-CF Bronchiectasis" study group. Patients were evaluated at baseline (T0) with questionnaires, spirometry, and sputum cultures, and followed for 12 months, with quarterly assessments. RESULTS: 82 patients were enrolled (mean age 16.1 ± 5.9 y). At T0, 21 had negative sputum, 41 were colonized, 20 had acute infection. After 12 months, 75% of colonized patients remained colonized, although the microorganism identified during follow-up was not necessarily the same as that detected at baseline, and 52% of negative patients remained negative. Among acute infection, 40% progressed to colonization and 40% became sputum-negative. No significant clinical or functional differences were observed among microbiological groups. The most common pathogens were S. aureus (acute 18%, colonization 33%), H. influenzae (acute 14%, colonization 33%), and P. aeruginosa (acute 9%, colonization 23%). Patients colonized with P. aeruginosa showed lower spirometric values and more extensive bronchiectasis. CONCLUSIONS: In PCD patients microbiological positivity is highly prevalent, being Haemophilus influenzae, Staphylococcus aureus, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa the most frequently isolated pathogens. Most patients colonized at baseline remained colonized over time and patients colonized by Pseudomonas aeruginosa tended to exhibit greater bronchiectasis extension and worse lung function.

papers.abstract_full: As biomedical research in space expands, microgravity and spaceflight-associated stressors are revealing cellular responses that may provide new insights into rare and severe metabolic and congenital disorders. Human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) and organoids are particularly promising as they enable patient-specific modelling in the space environment. In this review, we examine the current literature on space-based hiPSC experimental models, highlighting their relevance to pediatric disorders with well-defined genetic backgrounds, namely mitochondrial diseases and congenital heart disorders. We summarize the evidence that spaceflight conditions alter mitochondrial function, cytoskeletal organization, oxidative stress, calcium handling, cellular maturation, and gene expression, and discuss how these responses may converge with metabolic disease-associated phenotypes. We highlight both adaptive and pathological responses reported in space-based hiPSC studies and identify key experimental and mechanistic gaps. Finally, we consider how advances in stem cell technologies and space-based biomedical research may enable the development of personalized, patient-specific disease models and therapeutics for rare pediatric diseases, ultimately accelerating translational discovery and clinical innovation.

papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: Isolated gastric varices type I (IGV1) is a rare but severe manifestation of splenic vein thrombosis. While thrombophilia is a recognized cause, the underlying genetic determinants are often elusive. This study investigates the case of a proband presenting with IGV1, deep vein thrombosis (DVT), and Long QT syndrome Type 2 (LQT2), aiming to elucidate the genetic basis and functional impact of the identified SERPIND1 variants. METHODS: Whole-exome sequencing identified candidate variants in the proband, which were validated by Sanger sequencing. Functional assessment included quantifying SERPIND1 and KCNH2 mRNA in proband and control blood, analyzing heparin cofactor Ⅱ (HCⅡ) protein expression and localization in transfected 293T cells, and predicting the potential structural consequences of the variants using bioinformatic tools. RESULTS: The proband, a 31-year-old female, presented with isolated gastric fundal varices and a history of deep venous thrombosis (DVT), along with long QT syndrome type 2 (LQT2). Whole-exome sequencing (WES) identified two heterozygous variants, both confirmed by Sanger sequencing: a de novo SERPIND1 c.940 C > T (p.Arg314Trp) variant, classified as Pathogenic according to ACMG guidelines (PS2, PS3, PM2_Supporting, PP3), and a KCNH2 c.1707 C > A (p.Tyr569*) variant, also classified as Pathogenic (PVS1, PP1, PM2_Supporting) and showing familial co-segregation. The SERPIND1 variant was associated with reduced HCⅡ antigen levels and activity in plasma. In vitro assays revealed that both variants led to significantly reduced SERPIND1 and KCNH2 mRNA expression. In transfected cells, the SERPIND1 p.Arg314Trp variant markedly decreased HCⅡ protein levels and possibly induced aberrant nuclear mislocalization. Structural modeling suggested that the Arg314Trp substitution disrupts a key hydrogen bond within HCⅡ, while the KCNH2 p.Tyr569* nonsense variant is predicted to generate a truncated protein. CONCLUSION: The SERPIND1 c.940 C > T (p.Arg314Trp) variant is associated with reduced HCⅡ expression and functional impairment, which may contribute to a prothrombotic tendency in this patient. This study provides a hypothesis-generating observation supporting a potential role of HCⅡ deficiency in venous thrombosis and IGV1. The KCNH2 variant was accounted for the coexisting LQT2 phenotype.

papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: Acute type A aortic dissection during pregnancy is a rare but life-threatening condition, with an estimated incidence of approximately 4 cases per 1 million women aged 15-45 years. Hormonal and hemodynamic changes during pregnancy are factors that may predispose to aortic dissection. These changes begin in the first and second trimesters but are most pronounced in the third trimester and the early postpartum period. Genetic syndromes, such as Marfan syndrome, significantly increase the risk of aortic dissection. CASE PRESENTATION: A 41-year-old pregnant woman at 31 weeks of gestation with genetically confirmed Marfan syndrome presented with acute, severe, sharp retrosternal chest pain lasting four hours, radiating to the neck, accompanied by weakness and dizziness. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed dilation of the ascending aorta without significant aortic valve regurgitation. Computed tomography angiography confirmed the diagnosis of Stanford type A aortic dissection. Following a multidisciplinary team decision, an initial cesarean section with subsequent uterine artery embolization was performed, followed by emergency ascending aortic replacement. The patient and the newborn were successfully discharged on postoperative day 20. CONCLUSIONS: Although aortic dissection during pregnancy is rare, clinicians must maintain a high suspicion index for pregnant women presenting with severe chest pain. Careful monitoring of patients with suspected or confirmed connective tissue disorders is essential. This case demonstrates that acute type A aortic dissection may occur in pregnant patients with Marfan syndrome despite only moderate aortic root enlargement and highlights the value of rapid multidisciplinary management, including coordinated obstetric, endovascular, and cardiac surgical intervention.

papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: Myocardial recovery sufficient for left ventricular assist device (LVAD) explantation remains uncommon. Titin truncating variant (TTNtv)-associated cardiomyopathy demonstrates favorable reverse remodeling with medical therapy, but its remodeling potential during durable mechanical unloading is unknown. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective, single-center study of adults undergoing HeartMate 3 LVAD implantation from 2016-2025. Patients were categorized as TTNtv-associated cardiomyopathy, other genetically characterized nonischemic cardiomyopathy (NICM), or ischemic cardiomyopathy (ICM). The primary endpoint was absolute change in left ventricular end-systolic volume index (LVESVI) during LVAD support. Multivariable and sensitivity analyses evaluated potential confounding and influential observations. RESULTS: Among 51 patients, 7 had TTNtv-associated cardiomyopathy, 9 other NICM, and 35 ICM. TTNtv patients were younger than other NICM and ICM patients (40.5±15.8 vs 45.8±11.0 vs 67.4±9.3 years; P<0.001). Mean LVESVI decreased by 87.7±71.8 mL/m² in TTNtv patients compared with 30.4±28.3 mL/m² in other NICM and 32.6±30.6 mL/m² in ICM (P=0.039). Compared with ICM, TTNtv status remained associated with greater LVESVI reduction after adjustment for baseline LV end-diastolic diameter (β=-47.2 mL/m²; 95% CI, -75.9 to -18.4; P=0.002). Findings were directionally consistent across sensitivity analyses addressing age, post-LVAD guideline-directed medical therapy, follow-up duration, cardiomyopathy substrate, and influential observations. TTNtv patients more frequently met volumetric reverse remodeling criteria (85.7% vs 22.2% vs 57.1%; P=0.044). CONCLUSIONS: TTNtv-associated cardiomyopathy was associated with greater structural reverse remodeling during LVAD support, particularly LVESVI reduction. Although limited by the small TTNtv cohort and potential residual confounding, these hypothesis-generating findings suggest that genetic substrate may contribute to myocardial remodeling during mechanical unloading.

papers.abstract_full: Meniere disease (MD) is a rare inner ear disorder with a significant genetic contribution. We developed the MD classifier, an ML tool to distinguish familial from sporadic MD cases using rare variants in coding regions. We have generated a disease-specific gene variant score incorporating gene, variant, and disease-specific features. A gradient boosting classifier achieved the highest performance, with a test AUC of 0.843 (95% CI, 0.702-0.948) and an accuracy of 81.5%. Reclassification of sporadic cases into the familial group ranged from 16.6% to 28.3%. The model identified a burden of biallelic heterozygous variants suggesting hidden recessive inheritance that may affect up to 38% of MD patients. Gene-enrichment analysis using major classifier features revealed distinct biological pathways between familial and sporadic MD. This ML-based framework integrates unique genetic features that may improve the diagnostic yield of rare disorders and is universally applicable to conditions with both familial and sporadic phenotypes, enabling the identification of compound heterozygous recessive inheritance.

papers.abstract_full: Background:  Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is characterized by substantial heterogeneity in core symptom severity and co-occurring conditions, complicating efforts to understand its genetic basis. Most genetic studies rely on binary case-control ASD definitions, which may obscure clinically meaningful variation and distinct genetic contributions across the autism spectrum.  Methods: : We constructed machine learning (ML)-based categorical ASD subtypes and corresponding continuous ASD subtype scores using 14 key clinical symptom measures with adjustment of sex and age among 6,355 autistic children in the Simons Foundation Powering Autism Research for Knowledge (SPARK) cohort by Discriminative Dimensionality Reduction via learning a Tree (DDRTree). We then replicated and validated these subtypes and scores among 2,717 autistic children in the Simons Simplex Collection (SSC) using a modified k-nearest-neighbor (k-NN) approach. In SPARK and SSC, we further clinically validated the framework by examining associations of subtype classifications and scores with support needs, service utilization and medication use by regression models with adjustment for sex, age, genetic ancestry and socioeconomic factors. We further assessed SNP-based heritability, cell-type-specific heritability enrichment, polygenic scores (PGS) for psychiatric and cognitive traits, as well as rare copy-number variant (CNV) and  de novo variant (DNV) burdens across the ML-derived ASD subtype scores adjusting for sex, age and genetic ancestry.  Results: : We identified three clinically distinct ASD subtypes in SPARK varying in the types of supports utilized: a  high-support-needs (HSN) subtype characterized by broad developmental and functional impairments and very substantial support needs (OR = 1.63, P = 3.71 x 10  -98 ); an  emotional-behavioral-support-needs (EBSN) subtype marked by severe repetitive behaviors, elevated psychiatric comorbidity; and a  low-support-needs (LSN) subtype with milder symptoms and relatively lower overall support needs. The three groups were associated with differential patterns in the specific types of treatments that were most common for them, from higher intensity to lower intensity. Projected ASD subtypes and scores in SSC recapitulated the phenotypic and medication-use patterns observed in SPARK. SNP-based heritability was highest for the EBSN score (h  2 g = 0.224, SE = 0.051) followed by the HSN (h  2 g = 0.167, SE = 0.049) and LSN score (h  2 g = 0.064, SE = 0.044), with suggestive cell-type-specific heritability enrichments in fetal endodermal cells and adult motor neurons for EBSN score and fetal excitatory neurons and astrocytes for HSN score (both P Conclusions: : Our ML-based transferable ASD subtype framework captured clinically and genetically meaningful dimensions of ASD heterogeneity, warranting further validation in larger cohorts.  Keywords:  Autism spectrum disorder, phenotypic heterogeneity, subtypes, machine learning, genetic burden

papers.abstract_full: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia and a major cause of cardioembolic stroke. Although polygenic risk scores (PRS) are well characterized to quantify inherited susceptibility for AF, they provide limited insight into the pathways and tissues underlying genetic risk, which are critical to uncover for individual risk prediction. In this study, we develop a pathway-level multi-omics representation learning framework that converts individual genetic profiles into interpretable biological features by integrating GWAS-derived pathway burden scores with tissue-specific transcriptomic pathway signals. We constructed machine learning models to assess population-level AF risk prediction performance across genomic and transcriptomic tissue contexts; the pathway-based global attention models substantially improved risk prediction performance over PRS and other baselines (AUROC improved from 0.601 to 0.738). Transformer and graph neural network frameworks then assessed individual-level pathway interpretability, revealing heterogeneous contributions from electrical signaling, cardiac development, and DNA repair pathways to AF risk. This added interpretability highlights the potential of this pathway approach to enable more mechanistically informed risk stratification than static PRS by capturing underlying heterogeneity. To independently assess whether prioritized pathways reflected cardiac regulatory biology, we compared pathway rankings with transcriptional effects predicted by the AlphaGenome foundation model. Variants in highly ranked pathways showed significantly greater predicted effects on expression in atrial and ventricular tissues (FDR = 0.032) relative to controls, providing orthogonal evidence that the model identifies biologically relevant mechanisms. Overall, this work reframes polygenic risk from a single measure of susceptibility to tissue-informed pathway mechanisms, providing a framework for interpretable genomic stratification in complex diseases.

papers.abstract_full: OBJECTIVE: Obesity is a public health crisis with few effective preventative treatments limited by challenges in identifying who is at high risk of weight gain. To address this gap, our group has developed machine learning weight gain prediction models with modest predictive power. In this study, we aimed to build upon our prior work by incorporating a multi-ancestry polygenic risk score (MAPRS) into a machine learning model and hypothesized that its inclusion would improve weight gain prediction performance. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Adults aged 18-70 years with weight measurements 2 years apart were identified within the NIH All of Us Research Program. Participants with a history of cancer, bariatric surgery, or pregnancy were excluded. XGBoost machine learning models were developed using demographics, vitals, laboratory data, obesity-related comorbidities, and MAPRS. The primary outcome was total body weight (TBW) gain of ≥10% over 2 years. Performance was compared using the area under the curves (AUCs). RESULTS: The cohort consisted of 40 205 individuals (mean [SD] age 51.1[13.5] years; 56.1% female; 48.5% White, non-Hispanic), 3806 (9.5%) of whom gained ≥10% TBW over 2 years. Model performance with and without MAPRS was similar, with AUCs of 0.705 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.692-0.718) and 0.697 (0.683-0.710), respectively. Baseline age and MAPRS had the highest variable importance. The best net reclassification index was 0.7%, indicating marginal improvements in risk classification with MAPRS. DISCUSSION: Despite the known hereditary components of obesity and the strong association between the MAPRS and weight gain, incorporating a MAPRS did not substantially enhance model performance. CONCLUSION: Further optimization of integrating polygenic risk scores into machine learning weight gain prediction models is needed before they can be applied in the clinical setting.

papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: Sleep is a potentially modifiable behavioural factor that may influence breast cancer risk. This study examined the association between sleep patterns and incident breast cancer in relation to genetic susceptibility and plasma proteomic profiles. METHODS: This prospective cohort study included 159,452 UK Biobank women free of breast cancer at baseline. Sleep patterns were constructed from five sleep characteristics. Associations with incident breast cancer were assessed using Cox proportional hazards models and time-varying Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for demographic, socioeconomic, lifestyle, breast cancer-related, and clinical covariates. Kaplan-Meier curves, restricted cubic splines, and PRS-based joint and stratified analyses were performed. In the proteomic subcohort, differential expression, enrichment, and machine-learning-based feature prioritisation analyses were used to identify overlapping proteomic signatures related to sleep pattern and breast cancer status. RESULTS: During follow-up, 7,291 incident breast cancer cases were identified. Compared with a healthy sleep pattern, an unhealthy sleep pattern was associated with a higher risk of breast cancer in the fully adjusted model (HR = 1.10, 95% CI = 1.05-1.15). This association was consistent in time-varying Cox proportional hazards models (HR = 1.34, 95% CI = 1.02-1.77). Joint analyses showed that participants with both high PRS and an unhealthy sleep pattern had the highest breast cancer risk. Proteomic analyses identified overlapping protein signatures related to both sleep pattern and breast cancer status, with enrichment mainly in immune regulation, inflammatory signalling, vascular function, and extracellular matrix-related biological processes. Machine-learning-based feature prioritisation identified CRISP3, PADI2, PLA2G2A, SUSD4, TNFRSF6B, and UPK3A as key candidate proteins. CONCLUSIONS: Unhealthy sleep patterns were associated with increased incident breast cancer risk. Integrated genetic and proteomic analyses suggest that immune-inflammatory, vascular, and extracellular matrix-related processes may provide biological context for this association.

papers.abstract_full: Machine learning on marker-environment interactions boosts multi-trait genomic prediction across four crops and enables in silico design of cotton lines combining high yield, quality, and climate adaptability. Genomic selection (GS) accelerates breeding through early prediction of superior genotypes, but genotype-environment interactions (G×E) compromise yield stability and climate adaptation. Here, we employed machine learning to identify genome-wide loci associated with environmental responsiveness, phenotypic plasticity, and BLUP-adjusted traits, integrating them into core marker sets. Coupled with environmental covariates, these markers enabled GS models with improved cross-environment predictive accuracy. Evaluations across 13 phenotypic traits in four crops revealed LightGBM and random forest regression (RFR) as top performers, with LightGBM showing the most consistent superiority across scenarios, particularly in untested environments. In an in-silico genome-design analysis of cotton, SHAP-based interpretation within the fitted predictive model was used to propose candidate marker configurations: modification of 23-36 BLUP-associated markers in six elite fiber lines was predicted to improve boll weight (2.2-6.3%) and lint percentage (0.2-3.9%) in target environments, while additionally optimizing plasticity/environment-responsiveness markers yielded further predicted gains (3.5-7.2% and 2.3-3.5%, respectively). In 11 high-yield lines, modification of BLUP-associated markers was predicted to improve fiber length (0-2.4%) and strength (0.4-3.9%), with environment-interaction markers further enhancing traits (0.8-3.7%). Notably, 78-85% of environment-specific markers exhibited high SHAP values despite partial overlap with BLUP loci, suggesting their potential relevance to adaptive breeding. These improvements are derived from in silico model simulations and should be interpreted as candidate breeding targets rather than validated genetic gains. These results highlight machine learning as a pivotal tool for G × E-driven breeding strategies in multi-objective breeding to enable simultaneous optimization of yield, quality, and climate adaptability in crop improvement efforts.

papers.abstract_full: Abstract    Genomic selection has revolutionized the pace of crop breeding, but the cultivated potato (Solanum tuberosum, 2n = 4x = 48) still stands as a challenge: the accuracy of linear models like GBLUP, and of conventional deep learning is reduced by autotetrasomic inheritance, double-reduction, complex non-additive gene action, and small training populations. Approach: Results: We present QPotatoNet, a hybrid quantum–Transformer model that integrates a dosage-aware genomic Transformer encoder and a haplotype-block encoder with an 8-qubit variational quantum layer via cross-attention.tetrasomic SNP dosages and LD-defined phased haplotypes are simultaneously tokenized and processed to simultaneously predict genomic-estimated breeding values (GEBVs) for eight key agronomic traits. Results. On a 3,012-clone tetraploid panel (21,432 SNP loci), QPotatoNet attained a mean prediction accuracy of r = 0.734 across eight traits, improving on the best deep-learning baseline by 9.2% and on GBLUP by 22.6% on average, with the largest gains for low-heritability and non-additive traits. The variational quantum layer and the haplotype encoder led to the largest improve of accuracy in both cases when the ablation was executed. Conclusions. Through the integration of tetrasomic dosage structure and haplotype context into a quantum-enhanced attention mechanism, QPotatoNet closes the polyploid predictive gap and provides a feasible way for potato breeding cycle reduction.

papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND  The chromosome 9p21.3 locus is among the strongest genetic risk loci for cardiovascular disease (CVD), yet the regulatory mechanisms underlying this association remain poorly understood. Previous vascular disease studies focused predominantly on the role of this locus in smooth muscle cell (SMC) dysfunction, whereas its potential role in endothelial cells (ECs) remains less well characterized. Here, we sought to identify candidate regulatory variants at 9p21.3, their distal target genes, and effector transcripts that contribute to CVD-related phenotypes in ECs. METHODS  Promoter capture Hi-C was used to map chromatin interactions at 9p21.3 in primary human ascending aortic SMCs (n=6), supplementing the previously obtained ECs (n=16) dataset. To support the regulatory relevance of these interactions, expression quantitative trait locus analysis was performed in 136 vascular biopsies. Variant effects were prioritized  in silico using AlphaGenome. The regulatory activity of the prioritized region was validated using CRISPR activation.  RESULTS  Chromatin interaction mapping identified a complex regulatory architecture at the 9p21.3 locus involving 19 putative regulatory elements and 15 genes across ECs and SMCs.  MIR31HG showed the most recurrent distal promoter connectivity with the 9p21.3 region. Consistent with the chromatin interaction map, expression of  MIR31HG transcripts was associated with genetic variation at the 9p21.3 locus. In ECs, the lncRNA MIR31HG, but not miR-31, was responsive to hemodynamic flow. Depletion of  MIR31HG in ECs was associated with endothelial activation. Epigenetic tracks and deep learning predictions highlighted an active enhancer element at 9p21.3, which was subsequently validated by CRISPR activation and increased  MIR31HG expression, confirming its capacity to regulate  MIR31HG over a large genomic distance of approximately 538 kb.  CONCLUSIONS  Altogether, these data implicate lncRNA MIR31HG as a likely effector of the 9p21.3 CVD locus, linking the cis-regulatory element and heritable genetic variation in the respective region to endothelial activation through long-range enhancer regulation. Clinical Perspective  What Is New? Promoter capture Hi-C in primary human vascular cells identified recurrent long-range interactions between the 9p21.3 cardiovascular disease locus and the  MIR31HG promoter, extending the regulatory landscape beyond the nearest genes.  Expression of  MIR31HG transcripts was associated with 9p21.3 genetic variation in vascular tissue; the lncRNA MIR31HG was responsive to hemodynamic flow in endothelial cells and influenced the endothelial activation transcriptional programs upon depletion.  Integrated sequence-based, epigenomic, genetic, and CRISPR activation analyses nominated the 9p21.3 enhancer as a regulator of  MIR31HG in endothelial cells.  What Are the Clinical Implications? The findings suggest that the cardiovascular disease associations of 9p21.3 may involve stronger than previously anticipated endothelial regulatory mechanisms in addition to characterized effects in other vascular cell types. lncRNA MIR31HG provides a molecular link between noncoding genetic variation at 9p21.3 and endothelial cell-state regulation relevant to vascular disease.

papers.abstract_full: Polygenic risk scores (PRS) primarily rely on common variants because rare variant effects are difficult to estimate without large sequencing cohorts. We developed PRS-CARV, a summary statistics framework that integrates annotation-informed rare variant burden scores with common-variant PRS. In simulations, PRS-CARV consistently outperformed common-variant PRS alone. Applied to whole-genome sequencing data from the nuMoM2b-Heart Health Study, incorporating rare variants improved prediction of lipid traits by 2-11% compared with common-variant PRS. PRS-CARV enables practical integration of publicly available rare variant summary statistics, improving polygenic prediction and supporting broader implementation of precision medicine.

papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: Alzheimer's disease (AD), the most prevalent form of dementia, is highly heritable, yet much of its genetic basis remains unexplained. Most genetic studies have focused on European populations, with limited data from under-represented groups. Whole-exome sequencing (WES) in the Han Chinese population may help identify novel rare variants and population-specific genetic risk factors. AIMS: This study aims to use WES to identify potential candidate genes associated with dementia and AD in the Han Chinese population. METHODS: In this exploratory pilot study, we performed WES in 63 Han Chinese patients with dementia, including 43 with AD and 20 with non-AD dementia (including one with dementia with Lewy bodies, one with Parkinson's dementia, four with frontotemporal dementia and 14 with mixed dementia), to identify rare coding variants. Gene-based case-control burden analyses using public gnomAD controls were conducted in the overall dementia cohort and the AD subgroup. Protein-protein interaction, functional enrichment, weighted gene coexpression network analysis (WGCNA) and gene set variation analysis (GSVA) using single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) datasets were performed to evaluate biological relevance and cell-type-specific activity. Cell-type marker enrichment analysis was used to identify relevant neuronal subtypes. Multilevel evidence was integrated to prioritise candidate risk genes. RESULTS: We identified suggestive rare variant signals in genes involved in cilia-related pathways, with stronger signals in the AD subgroup. These candidate genes were enriched in WGCNA modules associated with ageing, microtubule organisation and dementia pathology. GSVA showed increased activity of candidate genes in astrocytes using the snRNA-seq dataset. Cell-type marker analysis revealed strong enrichment in Ex6 excitatory neurons. Finally, integration of multilevel evidence prioritised 10 candidate genes. CONCLUSIONS: This pilot study provides preliminary evidence that cilia-related pathways may be involved in dementia, especially AD susceptibility in the Han Chinese population. Further validation in larger independent cohorts with ancestry-matched controls and in functional experiments is required. Larger sample sizes for each dementia subtype will improve the detection of both dementia-shared and subtype-specific signals.

These candidate genes were enriched in WGCNA modules associated with ageing, microtubule organisation and dementia pathology.

papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: Prospective proteomic and proteogenomic studies may enhance the understanding of proteins associated with prostate cancer (PCa) development. METHODS: In a case-cohort study within the European Prospective Investigation into Cancer and Nutrition (EPIC), baseline plasma samples from 982 incident PCa cases and 1573 subcohort participants were profiled using the SomaScan 7k platform (over 6000 proteins). Associations were estimated using Prentice-weighted Cox models. The coprimary end points were incident overall PCa and aggressive PCa (n = 290). Findings were evaluated in the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities (ARIC) study and supported by Mendelian randomization (MR) and exome gene-burden analyses. KEY FINDINGS AND LIMITATIONS: ACP3, FLT4, and KLK3 were associated with overall PCa risk (hazard ratio [HR] per 1 standard deviation [SD] increase were 1.20 [1.10-1.31], 1.26 [1.13-1.40], and 2.28 [1.96-2.65], respectively). Seven proteins were associated with aggressive PCa risk, with ANKRD1 consistently associated across multiple clinically relevant disease subtypes. Twelve proteins were associated with PCa diagnosed >15 yr after blood draw, including ANXA2, GZMK, and OSCAR. ACP3, ANXA2, APOC2, and KLK3 showed consistent associations in both EPIC and ARIC. Additionally, four proteins had support from MR analyses and eight from rare-variant burden tests. Circulating products of established PCa driver genes, including ERBB3, KRAS, and NRAS, were associated with future aggressive disease. Limitations include incomplete external replication and differences in end point availability across cohorts. CONCLUSIONS AND CLINICAL IMPLICATIONS: Prospective plasma proteomic analyses identified circulating proteins associated with future PCa risk, including proteins related to immune, adhesion, angiogenesis, and PCa driver-gene pathways. These findings identify candidate protein risk factors for overall and clinically significant PCa, and warrant further validation and mechanistic evaluation.

papers.abstract_full: STUDY QUESTION: What are the genetic causes of asthenoteratozoospermia in consanguineous families, and what is the specific role of cilia- and flagella-associated proteins (CFAP) 46 in mammalian spermiogenesis? SUMMARY ANSWER: CFAP46 is a central apparatus protein essential for sperm flagellar assembly and head remodeling. WHAT IS KNOWN ALREADY: Asthenoteratozoospermia is a genetically heterogeneous condition characterized by reduced sperm motility and abnormal morphology. While several CFAPs are known to support axonemal organization, the functional role of CFAP46 in mammals remained uncharacterized prior to this study. STUDY DESIGN, SIZE, DURATION: We performed whole-genome or whole-exome sequencing on 13 consanguineous families affected by primary male infertility. Functional validation was conducted using three CRISPR/Cas9-engineered mouse models: a null allele, a FLAG-tagged knock-in, and a humanized patient-specific nonsense allele. PARTICIPANTS/MATERIALS, SETTING, METHODS: Genomic DNA from affected individuals and fertile relatives was analyzed by NGS and validated via Sanger sequencing. Mouse phenotypes were characterized through sperm analysis, immunofluorescence, and electron microscopy. Protein interactions were identified via immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry. Additionally, a gene-level burden analysis was applied to unresolved cases across 345 spermiogenesis-associated genes. MAIN RESULTS AND THE ROLE OF CHANCE: We identified homozygous loss-of-function variants in CFAP46, CFAP57, SEPTIN4, and SPEM2 segregating with infertility. Cfap46-deficient males were infertile due to significantly decreased sperm count, motility, and severe axonemal disruptions. CFAP46 was found to form an in vivo complex with CFAP54, CFAP74, and CFAP221. In families without a monogenic cause, affected individuals harbored a significantly higher burden of rare deleterious variants (4-16 genes) compared to fertile controls. LARGE SCALE DATA: Large-scale datasets and scripts are available via GitHub (https://github.com/sirusb/Nawaz_et_al_scripts). LIMITATIONS, REASONS FOR CAUTION: While functional mouse data strongly supports the identified variants, the rare-variant burden analysis identifies associations that require further functional validation to confirm specific oligogenic interactions. WIDER IMPLICATIONS OF THE FINDINGS: This study establishes CFAP46 as a regulator of mammalian spermiogenesis and suggests that, beyond monogenic defects, aggregated rare-variant burden may also contribute to male infertility. These findings refine the genetic basis of asthenoteratozoospermia, supporting precise molecular diagnosis, individualized prognostic counseling, and informed use of assisted reproduction (e.g. ICSI) in affected couples. papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: Chronic pain is a major global health burden with a substantial but incompletely understood genetic basis. Although genome-wide association studies have identified multiple common-variant loci for pain-related traits, the contribution of rare coding variants to chronic pain susceptibility, biological mechanisms, and shared architecture across pain phenotypes remains unclear. METHODS: We performed an exome-wide association study across ten chronic pain phenotypes using whole-exome sequencing data from 327,642 European participants in the UK Biobank. Variant-level and gene-level association analyses were conducted to identify common and rare coding signals. Downstream analyses included conditional analysis, statistical fine-mapping, validation in non-European populations, replication in independent cohorts, cross-trait meta-analysis, colocalization, pathway and tissue enrichment, single-cell enrichment, summary-data-based Mendelian randomization, and estimation of heritability and genetic correlation from common and rare variants. RESULTS: We identified 286 significant variant-level associations arising from 235 unique variants mapped to 117 genes, including 13 novel lead variants and 44 independent lead signals. Gene-level analyses identified ten significant genes driven predominantly by rare functional variants: ADAMTSL5, ANKRD12, ARID5A, DPP7, GMCL1, HCK, KIF20B, SLC13A1, UBR2, and ZNF558. Functional analyses implicated pathways related to nervous system development, axonogenesis, and synaptic organization, with enrichment in brain tissues and hTRPM8-expressing dorsal root ganglion neurons. Mendelian randomization analyses highlighted convergent regulatory effects across neural and immune-related tissues. Heritability analyses showed that rare coding variants explained a modest proportion of variance relative to common variants but exhibited larger average effects in the most damaging functional classes, particularly high-confidence loss-of-function variants. Genetic correlation analyses revealed shared genetic components among chronic pain conditions and positive correlations with selected psychiatric and nervous system disorders. CONCLUSIONS: These findings provide a comprehensive map of coding variation underlying chronic pain and show that both common and rare coding variants contribute to its genetic architecture. Rare coding variants explain only a limited fraction of heritability but offer strong mechanistic insight by implicating discrete genes and pathways related to neuronal development, neuroimmune signaling, and tissue homeostasis. This work advances understanding of chronic pain biology and provides a foundation for future multi-ancestry studies and functional validation.

papers.abstract_full: Stabilizing selection is thought to maintain quantitative traits near evolutionary optima, yet the extent to which it constrains human molecular phenotypes remains largely unknown. Here, we investigate stabilizing selection on 2’923 plasma proteins by triangulating complementary signatures operating across evolutionary timescales in up to 54’000 UK Biobank participants. We contrasted genetic signatures reflecting selective constraint accumulated over generations with phenotypic evidence that deviations in protein abundance are associated with reduced contemporary fitness-related outcomes. Historical selection was assessed from the frequency-dependent architecture of protein levels using genome-wide common variants with LDpred2 and a newly developed rare loss-of-function burden framework. Contemporary evidence was obtained from quadratic associations between protein abundance and three fitness proxies: reproductive success, somatic health, and parental longevity. Among significant estimates, 100% and 92.4% supported stabilizing selection in the common- and rare-variant-based analysis, respectively, compared to 99.8% for somatic health, 97.7% for parental longevity, and 89.3% for reproductive success. Despite capturing distinct timescales and aspects of selection, the approaches showed convergence. Rare-variant-based estimates showed concordance with health-score-derived coefficients (  ρ = 0.36,  p = 5.2  × 10  − 6 ) and with independent measures of evolutionary constraint, including protein heritability (  ρ = 0.20,  p = 5.2  × 10  − 5 ), loss-of-function intolerance (  ρ =  − 0.19,  p = 6.1  × 10  − 5 ), and cross-species transcript evolutionary rate (  ρ = 0.15,  p = 2.4  × 10  − 2 ). Our results suggest that stabilizing selection is a pervasive force shaping the human plasma proteome and demonstrate that integrating genetic architecture with fitness-related consequences can connect long-term evolutionary constraint with contemporary phenotypic variation.
