selected_papers.abstract_full: Folate deficiency is associated with increased risk of conotruncal heart defects (CTHD), but its interaction with genetic factors remains unclear. Our objective was to investigate genome-wide associations between common genetic variants and birth before versus after universal folic acid fortification among children with CTHD and other heart defects. Sequencing data were available through the Pediatric Cardiac Genomics Consortium, aligned to the human reference genome (GRCh38/hg38), and jointly processed to ensure uniform variant detection and minimize batch effects. Analyses were restricted to individuals with European-inferred genetic ancestry, limiting generalizability to other ancestral groups. Genome-wide association study (GWAS) models compared allele frequencies across fortification eras among all participants (n = 1285), the subset with CTHD (n = 534), and the remaining individuals with other heart defects (n = 751). Functional enrichment was assessed using the Database for Annotation, Visualization and Integrated Discovery (DAVID). Among the full analytic group, eight loci had at least two suggestive variants before compared to after fortification. Among the subset with CTHD, two variants located in DHRS3 (rs7551703, odds ratio [OR] 2.10, and rs6541043, OR 2.21) and four variants located in PPARGC1B showed suggestive association after fortification (OR 4.47-4.51). Enriched biological pathway terms were consistent with cardiac developmental processes. In summary, this study examined the association between folic acid fortification and genetic risk for CTHD and other heart defects and identified associations with fortification era that suggest some shift in risk following fortification. Identified pathways suggest gene-nutrient interactions may modulate cardiac developmental pathways, underscoring the relationship between maternal folate status and cardiovascular development.

selected_papers.abstract: Large-scale genetic variant analysis involves multiple computational steps, data formats, gene and variant annotation sources and compute requirements. Some of the steps like joint calling for large cohorts are run on large compute clusters, while gene/variant classification algorithms can be run in a desktop computer. At the same time, variant annotations such as gene expression and gene constraints metrics from gnomAD are provided in different formats, by resources that frequently change their…
selected_papers.abstract_full: Large-scale genetic variant analysis involves multiple computational steps, data formats, gene and variant annotation sources and compute requirements. Some of the steps like joint calling for large cohorts are run on large compute clusters, while gene/variant classification algorithms can be run in a desktop computer. At the same time, variant annotations such as gene expression and gene constraints metrics from gnomAD are provided in different formats, by resources that frequently change their versions. Here, we present  hvantk , a framework that provides a common data model for large-scale annotation and analysis of genetic variants, by extending popular data formats such as Hail MatrixTable and AnnData. hvantk agentically integrates 21 public multi-omic data providers as plugins that a developer, bioinformatician or an AI agent can author without modifying the framework’s core, drives analysis workflows using agent skills, and scales from single desktop computers to high-performance computing clusters. We used hvantk for reanalysing three case-control cohorts, comprising congenital heart disease (CHD), developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (Epi25) and schizophrenia (SCHEMA). Re-ranking of gene-based burden testing results using multi-omic annotations improved the recovery of curated disease genes from 26% to 49% in CHD, 40% to 48% in Epi25 and 51% to 54% in SCHEMA, among the top decile re-ranked genes. Expression at bulk and single-cell levels were the features contributing the most over a baseline of burden, gene constraint and publication count.

selected_papers.abstract_full: Background  Hypoplastic Left Heart Syndrome (HLHS) is a severe congenital heart defect characterized by underdevelopment of left-sided cardiac structures, requiring staged surgical palliation that establishes the right ventricle as the single ventricle maintaining systemic circulation. After surgery, patients remain highly susceptible to heart failure, possibly due to the increased hemodynamic load imposed on the single surviving ventricle. Because the etiology of HLHS remains poorly understood, elucidating the mechanisms that drive ventricular dysfunction requires model systems that capture both patient-specific genetics and the dynamic mechanical environment of the ventricle. Thus, our objective was to compare how induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived cardiomyocytes (iPSC-CMs) from patients with HLHS differ from control in static culture and in response to cyclic stretch. Methods  Control iPSCs from two unaffected donors and iPSCs from four HLHS patients were differentiated into iPSC-CMs, engineered into aligned tissues, and cultured statically or exposed to cyclic 20% uniaxial stretch at 1 Hz for 48h. Sarcomere organization was quantified in static tissues using images of immunostained α-actinin. Calcium transients at 1 Hz pacing frequency in static and stretched tissues were evaluated using Fluo-4 calcium indicator dye. Bulk RNA sequencing was performed to evaluate stretch-induced transcriptomic changes in control and HLHS iPSC-CMs. Results  In static culture, HLHS iPSC-CMs had modest defects in sarcomere organization and calcium transient morphology compared to control. In response to cyclic stretch, control iPSC-CMs exhibited calcium transients with quicker rise time, a response observed in only one of four lines of HLHS iPSC-CMs. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that all four lines of HLHS iPSC-CMs failed to upregulate calcium handling and sarcomere-associated genes in response to stretch, unlike control iPSC-CMs. Stretch also induced HLHS iPSC-CMs to exhibit pronounced activation of inflammatory signaling pathways, a response not observed in control iPSC-CMs. Conclusions  iPSC-CMs from HLHS patients demonstrate aberrant responses to cyclic stretch, including blunted adaptation of calcium transients and heightened inflammatory signaling. These findings implicate defective mechanoadaptation as a potential contributor to single ventricle failure and identify potential candidate biomarkers and new opportunities for therapeutic interventions for HLHS patients.

selected_papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: Mental disorders and heart failure frequently co-occur, but their shared genetic architecture remains incompletely understood. METHODS: Prospective Cox regression analysis in the UK Biobank (UKB) quantified the risk of incident heart failure associated with mental disorders. Linkage disequilibrium score regression estimated genetic correlations, while multitrait genome-wide association and cross-phenotype association analyses identified candidate pleiotropic loci. Statistical fine mapping and gene-level association analyses prioritized candidate variants and genes. Bayesian colocalization assessed evidence for shared candidate variants, and exploratory Gene Ontology biological-process overrepresentation analysis provided descriptive biological context. Single-cell RNA sequencing and genetically informed spatial mapping (gsMap) provided cellular and spatial context for prioritized genes. Geneformer-based in silico perturbation analysis was performed using a cardiac cell atlas of dilated cardiomyopathy to prioritize candidate pleiotropic genes and identify cardiac cell states showing predicted embedding shifts. RESULTS: Prospective UKB analyses demonstrated that mental disorders, such as posttraumatic stress disorder, depression, and bipolar disorder, were associated with a higher risk of incident heart failure. Multitrait analysis identified 607 pleiotropic variants, with fine-mapping and colocalization converging on prioritized candidate loci, including TMEM18, NKX2-2, and XRN2. Single-cell expression profiling and spatial mapping provided context at the cellular and tissue levels for the prioritized genes. Geneformer-based in silico perturbation prioritized FOXP1 and TMEM106B as leading pleiotropic candidate genes on the basis of their predicted changes in downstream gene embeddings in cardiac cellular contexts. CONCLUSIONS: This study identifies shared genetic architecture between mental disorders and heart failure and prioritizes candidate pleiotropic genes associated with both. Transcriptomic and in silico perturbation analyses provide exploratory cellular, spatial, and cardiac functional context. Functional validation is required before mechanistic or therapeutic interpretation.

selected_papers.abstract_full: PURPOSE OF REVIEW: This review aims to evaluate the contemporary and evolving role of cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging in arrhythmic risk stratification for patients with non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy, specifically focussing on dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) and non-dilated left ventricular cardiomyopathy (NDLVC). This review synthesises current data on late gadolinium enhancement (LGE), parametric mapping, strain imaging and artificial intelligence (AI), and contextualises these among emerging genetic risk stratification approaches. RECENT FINDINGS: Left ventricular ejection fraction has been the cornerstone for guideline-based arrhythmic risk stratification in patients with DCM, despite limited precision. Observational data and meta-analyses have established the presence of replacement fibrosis through LGE-CMR as a powerful independent predictor of ventricular arrhythmias (VAs) and sudden cardiac death. Crucially, the absence of LGE identifies a low-risk cohort. Much recent focus has been on understanding whether more precise characterisation of scar can further enhance arrhythmic risk stratification, for example through scar quantification. Although data exists supporting a potential role for T1 mapping for arrhythmic risk prediction in this cohort, further research is required to support its widespread adoption. Emerging multimodal approaches using artificial intelligence and personalised computational "digital twins" are areas of important interest, offering scope for integration of imaging, electrocardiographic and genomic data layers. Arrhythmic risk stratification in non-ischaemic cardiomyopathies remains challenging despite significant advances. Progressive refinement in precision has accompanied a shift from a restrictive, functional assessment towards an integrated, substrate-driven precision model. CMR represents the cornerstone of this evolution.

selected_papers.abstract_full: IMPORTANCE: Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) is a major cause of heart failure that disproportionately affects individuals of predominantly African ancestry, among whom familial clustering of disease is more pronounced relative to those of predominantly European ancestry. Truncating variants in TTN, which encodes the sarcomeric protein titin, are the most common established monogenic cause of DCM. A common CD36 nonsense variant enriched among individuals of African ancestry has also been shown to account for a substantial burden of DCM. OBJECTIVE: To compare the contribution of a CD36 nonsense variant to DCM risk with that of truncating variants in TTN and pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in other established genes for DCM. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: Multicohort genetic association study including participants of African and European ancestry with exome or genome sequence data and DCM case status from the following 4 US datasets: All of Us Research Program (recruitment: 2017-present; last follow-up: August 27, 2024), Million Veteran Program (recruitment: 2011-present; last follow-up: September 30, 2024), Penn Medicine Biobank (recruitment: 2013-present; last follow-up: November 14, 2022), and the DCM Precision Medicine Study (recruitment: 2016-2020; last follow-up: March 15, 2020). EXPOSURE: Carrier status for TTN truncating variants, pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in 11 high-confidence genes for DCM, and the nonsense variant CD36 Y325* (0, 1, or 2 copies). MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Risk of DCM, prevalence of variant carriers among DCM cases, and population attributable fraction of DCM. RESULTS: Among 82 623 individuals of predominantly African ancestry across 4 cohorts, the mean age was 53.4 years (SD, 13.9 years), 47 124 were male, and 1316 had DCM. Individuals who were homozygous for the CD36 Y325* risk allele had a higher risk of DCM (odds ratio [OR], 4.8; 95% CI, 3.1-7.3) as did those who were heterozygous (OR, 1.4; 95% CI, 1.2-1.7). TTN truncating variants also conferred an elevated risk of DCM in participants of African ancestry (OR, 8.5; 95% CI, 5.5-13.0). Among 1316 individuals of African ancestry classified as DCM cases, 33 (2.5%) were homozygous for CD36, 56 (4.3%) had TTN truncating variants, and 16 (1.2%) had pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in other high-confidence genes for DCM. In population-level analyses incorporating both heterozygous and homozygous CD36 Y325* carriers, the population attributable fraction for CD36 (9.0% [6.2% for heterozygous carriers and 2.8% for homozygous carriers]) surpassed the population attributable fraction for TTN truncating variants (3.7%). CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In 4 US cohorts, an ancestry-specific CD36 variant contributed more to DCM burden among individuals of African ancestry than established genes for DCM, including TTN truncating variants that are typically considered the most common genetic cause. These findings reshape the known genetic architecture of DCM in individuals of African ancestry and highlight the importance of representation in genomic research.

selected_papers.abstract_full: Meniere disease (MD) is a rare inner ear disorder with a significant genetic contribution. We developed the MD classifier, an ML tool to distinguish familial from sporadic MD cases using rare variants in coding regions. We have generated a disease-specific gene variant score incorporating gene, variant, and disease-specific features. A gradient boosting classifier achieved the highest performance, with a test AUC of 0.843 (95% CI, 0.702-0.948) and an accuracy of 81.5%. Reclassification of sporadic cases into the familial group ranged from 16.6% to 28.3%. The model identified a burden of biallelic heterozygous variants suggesting hidden recessive inheritance that may affect up to 38% of MD patients. Gene-enrichment analysis using major classifier features revealed distinct biological pathways between familial and sporadic MD. This ML-based framework integrates unique genetic features that may improve the diagnostic yield of rare disorders and is universally applicable to conditions with both familial and sporadic phenotypes, enabling the identification of compound heterozygous recessive inheritance.

selected_papers.abstract_full: Background:  Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is characterized by substantial heterogeneity in core symptom severity and co-occurring conditions, complicating efforts to understand its genetic basis. Most genetic studies rely on binary case-control ASD definitions, which may obscure clinically meaningful variation and distinct genetic contributions across the autism spectrum.  Methods: : We constructed machine learning (ML)-based categorical ASD subtypes and corresponding continuous ASD subtype scores using 14 key clinical symptom measures with adjustment of sex and age among 6,355 autistic children in the Simons Foundation Powering Autism Research for Knowledge (SPARK) cohort by Discriminative Dimensionality Reduction via learning a Tree (DDRTree). We then replicated and validated these subtypes and scores among 2,717 autistic children in the Simons Simplex Collection (SSC) using a modified k-nearest-neighbor (k-NN) approach. In SPARK and SSC, we further clinically validated the framework by examining associations of subtype classifications and scores with support needs, service utilization and medication use by regression models with adjustment for sex, age, genetic ancestry and socioeconomic factors. We further assessed SNP-based heritability, cell-type-specific heritability enrichment, polygenic scores (PGS) for psychiatric and cognitive traits, as well as rare copy-number variant (CNV) and  de novo variant (DNV) burdens across the ML-derived ASD subtype scores adjusting for sex, age and genetic ancestry.  Results: : We identified three clinically distinct ASD subtypes in SPARK varying in the types of supports utilized: a  high-support-needs (HSN) subtype characterized by broad developmental and functional impairments and very substantial support needs (OR = 1.63, P = 3.71 x 10  -98 ); an  emotional-behavioral-support-needs (EBSN) subtype marked by severe repetitive behaviors, elevated psychiatric comorbidity; and a  low-support-needs (LSN) subtype with milder symptoms and relatively lower overall support needs. The three groups were associated with differential patterns in the specific types of treatments that were most common for them, from higher intensity to lower intensity. selected_papers.abstract_full: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia and a major cause of cardioembolic stroke. Although polygenic risk scores (PRS) are well characterized to quantify inherited susceptibility for AF, they provide limited insight into the pathways and tissues underlying genetic risk, which are critical to uncover for individual risk prediction. In this study, we develop a pathway-level multi-omics representation learning framework that converts individual genetic profiles into interpretable biological features by integrating GWAS-derived pathway burden scores with tissue-specific transcriptomic pathway signals. We constructed machine learning models to assess population-level AF risk prediction performance across genomic and transcriptomic tissue contexts; the pathway-based global attention models substantially improved risk prediction performance over PRS and other baselines (AUROC improved from 0.601 to 0.738). Transformer and graph neural network frameworks then assessed individual-level pathway interpretability, revealing heterogeneous contributions from electrical signaling, cardiac development, and DNA repair pathways to AF risk. This added interpretability highlights the potential of this pathway approach to enable more mechanistically informed risk stratification than static PRS by capturing underlying heterogeneity. To independently assess whether prioritized pathways reflected cardiac regulatory biology, we compared pathway rankings with transcriptional effects predicted by the AlphaGenome foundation model. Variants in highly ranked pathways showed significantly greater predicted effects on expression in atrial and ventricular tissues (FDR = 0.032) relative to controls, providing orthogonal evidence that the model identifies biologically relevant mechanisms. Overall, this work reframes polygenic risk from a single measure of susceptibility to tissue-informed pathway mechanisms, providing a framework for interpretable genomic stratification in complex diseases.

selected_papers.abstract_full: OBJECTIVE: Obesity is a public health crisis with few effective preventative treatments limited by challenges in identifying who is at high risk of weight gain. To address this gap, our group has developed machine learning weight gain prediction models with modest predictive power. In this study, we aimed to build upon our prior work by incorporating a multi-ancestry polygenic risk score (MAPRS) into a machine learning model and hypothesized that its inclusion would improve weight gain prediction performance. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Adults aged 18-70 years with weight measurements 2 years apart were identified within the NIH All of Us Research Program. Participants with a history of cancer, bariatric surgery, or pregnancy were excluded. XGBoost machine learning models were developed using demographics, vitals, laboratory data, obesity-related comorbidities, and MAPRS. The primary outcome was total body weight (TBW) gain of ≥10% over 2 years. Performance was compared using the area under the curves (AUCs). RESULTS: The cohort consisted of 40 205 individuals (mean [SD] age 51.1[13.5] years; 56.1% female; 48.5% White, non-Hispanic), 3806 (9.5%) of whom gained ≥10% TBW over 2 years. Model performance with and without MAPRS was similar, with AUCs of 0.705 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.692-0.718) and 0.697 (0.683-0.710), respectively. Baseline age and MAPRS had the highest variable importance. The best net reclassification index was 0.7%, indicating marginal improvements in risk classification with MAPRS. DISCUSSION: Despite the known hereditary components of obesity and the strong association between the MAPRS and weight gain, incorporating a MAPRS did not substantially enhance model performance. CONCLUSION: Further optimization of integrating polygenic risk scores into machine learning weight gain prediction models is needed before they can be applied in the clinical setting.

selected_papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: Sleep is a potentially modifiable behavioural factor that may influence breast cancer risk. This study examined the association between sleep patterns and incident breast cancer in relation to genetic susceptibility and plasma proteomic profiles. METHODS: This prospective cohort study included 159,452 UK Biobank women free of breast cancer at baseline. Sleep patterns were constructed from five sleep characteristics. Associations with incident breast cancer were assessed using Cox proportional hazards models and time-varying Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for demographic, socioeconomic, lifestyle, breast cancer-related, and clinical covariates. Kaplan-Meier curves, restricted cubic splines, and PRS-based joint and stratified analyses were performed. In the proteomic subcohort, differential expression, enrichment, and machine-learning-based feature prioritisation analyses were used to identify overlapping proteomic signatures related to sleep pattern and breast cancer status. RESULTS: During follow-up, 7,291 incident breast cancer cases were identified. Compared with a healthy sleep pattern, an unhealthy sleep pattern was associated with a higher risk of breast cancer in the fully adjusted model (HR = 1.10, 95% CI = 1.05-1.15). This association was consistent in time-varying Cox proportional hazards models (HR = 1.34, 95% CI = 1.02-1.77). Joint analyses showed that participants with both high PRS and an unhealthy sleep pattern had the highest breast cancer risk. Proteomic analyses identified overlapping protein signatures related to both sleep pattern and breast cancer status, with enrichment mainly in immune regulation, inflammatory signalling, vascular function, and extracellular matrix-related biological processes. Machine-learning-based feature prioritisation identified CRISP3, PADI2, PLA2G2A, SUSD4, TNFRSF6B, and UPK3A as key candidate proteins. CONCLUSIONS: Unhealthy sleep patterns were associated with increased incident breast cancer risk. Integrated genetic and proteomic analyses suggest that immune-inflammatory, vascular, and extracellular matrix-related processes may provide biological context for this association.

selected_papers.abstract_full: Machine learning on marker-environment interactions boosts multi-trait genomic prediction across four crops and enables in silico design of cotton lines combining high yield, quality, and climate adaptability. Genomic selection (GS) accelerates breeding through early prediction of superior genotypes, but genotype-environment interactions (G×E) compromise yield stability and climate adaptation. Here, we employed machine learning to identify genome-wide loci associated with environmental responsiveness, phenotypic plasticity, and BLUP-adjusted traits, integrating them into core marker sets. Coupled with environmental covariates, these markers enabled GS models with improved cross-environment predictive accuracy. Evaluations across 13 phenotypic traits in four crops revealed LightGBM and random forest regression (RFR) as top performers, with LightGBM showing the most consistent superiority across scenarios, particularly in untested environments. In an in-silico genome-design analysis of cotton, SHAP-based interpretation within the fitted predictive model was used to propose candidate marker configurations: modification of 23-36 BLUP-associated markers in six elite fiber lines was predicted to improve boll weight (2.2-6.3%) and lint percentage (0.2-3.9%) in target environments, while additionally optimizing plasticity/environment-responsiveness markers yielded further predicted gains (3.5-7.2% and 2.3-3.5%, respectively). In 11 high-yield lines, modification of BLUP-associated markers was predicted to improve fiber length (0-2.4%) and strength (0.4-3.9%), with environment-interaction markers further enhancing traits (0.8-3.7%). Notably, 78-85% of environment-specific markers exhibited high SHAP values despite partial overlap with BLUP loci, suggesting their potential relevance to adaptive breeding. These improvements are derived from in silico model simulations and should be interpreted as candidate breeding targets rather than validated genetic gains. These results highlight machine learning as a pivotal tool for G × E-driven breeding strategies in multi-objective breeding to enable simultaneous optimization of yield, quality, and climate adaptability in crop improvement efforts.

selected_papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND  The chromosome 9p21.3 locus is among the strongest genetic risk loci for cardiovascular disease (CVD), yet the regulatory mechanisms underlying this association remain poorly understood. Previous vascular disease studies focused predominantly on the role of this locus in smooth muscle cell (SMC) dysfunction, whereas its potential role in endothelial cells (ECs) remains less well characterized. Here, we sought to identify candidate regulatory variants at 9p21.3, their distal target genes, and effector transcripts that contribute to CVD-related phenotypes in ECs. METHODS  Promoter capture Hi-C was used to map chromatin interactions at 9p21.3 in primary human ascending aortic SMCs (n=6), supplementing the previously obtained ECs (n=16) dataset. To support the regulatory relevance of these interactions, expression quantitative trait locus analysis was performed in 136 vascular biopsies. Variant effects were prioritized  in silico using AlphaGenome. The regulatory activity of the prioritized region was validated using CRISPR activation.  RESULTS  Chromatin interaction mapping identified a complex regulatory architecture at the 9p21.3 locus involving 19 putative regulatory elements and 15 genes across ECs and SMCs.  MIR31HG showed the most recurrent distal promoter connectivity with the 9p21.3 region. Consistent with the chromatin interaction map, expression of  MIR31HG transcripts was associated with genetic variation at the 9p21.3 locus. In ECs, the lncRNA MIR31HG, but not miR-31, was responsive to hemodynamic flow. Depletion of  MIR31HG in ECs was associated with endothelial activation. Epigenetic tracks and deep learning predictions highlighted an active enhancer element at 9p21.3, which was subsequently validated by CRISPR activation and increased  MIR31HG expression, confirming its capacity to regulate  MIR31HG over a large genomic distance of approximately 538 kb.  CONCLUSIONS  Altogether, these data implicate lncRNA MIR31HG as a likely effector of the 9p21.3 CVD locus, linking the cis-regulatory element and heritable genetic variation in the respective region to endothelial activation through long-range enhancer regulation. Clinical Perspective  What Is New? Promoter capture Hi-C in primary human vascular cells identified recurrent long-range interactions between the 9p21.3 cardiovascular disease locus and the  MIR31HG promoter, extending the regulatory landscape beyond the nearest genes.  Expression of  MIR31HG transcripts was associated with 9p21.3 genetic variation in vascular tissue; the lncRNA MIR31HG was responsive to hemodynamic flow in endothelial cells and influenced the endothelial activation transcriptional programs upon depletion.  Integrated sequence-based, epigenomic, genetic, and CRISPR activation analyses nominated the 9p21.3 enhancer as a regulator of  MIR31HG in endothelial cells.  What Are the Clinical Implications? The findings suggest that the cardiovascular disease associations of 9p21.3 may involve stronger than previously anticipated endothelial regulatory mechanisms in addition to characterized effects in other vascular cell types. lncRNA MIR31HG provides a molecular link between noncoding genetic variation at 9p21.3 and endothelial cell-state regulation relevant to vascular disease.

selected_papers.abstract_full: Diabetic cardiomyopathy (DCM) is a distinct myocardial disease defined by the existence of abnormal myocardial structure and performance in diabetes mellitus patients without hypertension and coronary artery disease. DCM has been identified as a major cause of heart failure, hospitalisation and cardiovascular mortality with increasing global burden of diabetes. However, there is a large interindividual variation in disease susceptibility, disease progression and response to therapy, highlighting the limitations of conventional management strategies that are applied uniformly. Precision medicine provides a transformational approach through the integration of genomic, molecular, imaging, clinical and lifestyle data to allow for personalized risk assessment, early diagnosis, prognostication and treatment. This review presents the recent advances in the field of precision medicine for DCM with a focus on the molecular pathological mechanisms including metabolic disorders, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, inflammation, fibrosis and microvascular injury. We discuss the relevance of genomics, pharmacogenomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, lipidomics and epigenomics in the context of disease heterogeneity and identification of novel therapeutic targets. Emerging biomarkers including circulating microRNAs, non-coding RNAs, inflammatory mediators, fibrosis-related markers and extracellular vesicles are discussed for their potential in personal diagnosis and prognosis. We also consider the increasing role of advanced cardiac imaging, digital phenotyping, wearable technologies, artificial intelligence, and machine learning in enhancing early detection and clinical decision-making. In this review, the therapeutic advances, including sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors, glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists, anti-fibrotic therapies, mitochondrial-targeted interventions, regenerative medicine, gene therapy, and RNA-based therapeutics, are discussed, with a focus on the precision medicine approach. Finally, we present current challenges in data integration, clinical validation, cost-effectiveness, and ethical issues, and highlight future directions in digital twins, multi-omics integration, and AI-driven personalized cardiology. The combination of these technologies has the potential to revolutionize the prevention and management of diabetic cardiomyopathy and improve cardiovascular outcomes in patients with diabetes.

selected_papers.abstract_full: Isolated focal dystonia is a rare movement disorder characterized by abnormalities in brain structure and function. The genes underlying isolated focal dystonia are not fully elucidated, and genetic studies are constrained by incomplete penetrance and small family sizes. Neuroimaging endophenotypes shared by patients and unaffected relatives can reveal genetic liability independently of clinical manifestation and offer a strategy for advancing gene discovery. We developed DystoniaGeneNet, a 3D convolutional neural network that predicts familial status from T1-weighted brain MRIs. We then used its predictions to guide genetic analyses in isolated focal dystonia. DystoniaGeneNet was trained on 40 patients with familial laryngeal dystonia and 40 healthy controls, then applied to independent cohorts of 21 patients with familial isolated focal dystonia, 364 patients with sporadic dystonia, and 98 unaffected relatives. Model predictions were incorporated into variant prioritization and segregation analysis in 214 individuals with whole-exome sequencing data, and results were replicated in another 738 independent exomes, in genetic data from a hospital-based biobank (892 dystonia cases, 2,475 controls), and in the  All of Us Research Program genetic data (1,343 dystonia cases, 6,840 controls). DystoniaGeneNet discriminated familial dystonia from healthy controls in the training set and correctly classified 85.7% of independent familial cases, using a biomarker centred on the corpus callosum and inferior temporal gyrus. Across the discovery and replication cohorts, we identified rare, likely pathogenic genetic variants in  RAP1GAP and  TNN segregating with disease in families. Additional variants were found in singletons with isolated focal dystonia. In patients with clinically sporadic dystonia but predicted to have familial features, we observed multiple rare variants in  ITSN2 , including three high-confidence loss-of-function variants, and an enrichment of damaging missense variants in its Dbl homology domain. To determine the functional impact of discovered genetic variants, we assessed gene expression and splicing via qPCR and RNA sequencing (  n = 74), revealing reduced  RAP1GAP and  ITSN2 expression in variant carriers. At the pathway level, rare nonsynonymous variants in brain-expressed matrisome genes were associated with dystonia (  P = 0.012). Our strategy utilizing a deep learning-derived neuroimaging endophenotype to empower gene discovery uncovered  RAP1GAP, TNN , and  ITSN2 as novel genes associated with isolated focal dystonia. These genes converge on perisynaptic extracellular matrix-synapse signalling, implicating a mechanism linked to synaptic plasticity deficits, and identifying a molecular substrate for network-level brain abnormalities that characterize this disorder. Further, we exemplify a generalizable framework for leveraging endophenotypes in rare neurogenetic diseases with incomplete penetrance.

selected_papers.abstract_full: Biobank-scale imaging-genomic cohorts enable genome-wide association studies (GWASs) of organ structure and function. Traditional approaches rely on expert-defined image-derived phenotypes (IDPs), which capture only a fraction of the biological variation in high-content images. Powered by artificial intelligence, self-supervised learning (SSL) learns representations directly from intrinsic image structures, creating scalable, data-driven traits. Here, we review the technical frameworks and challenges of SSL-based imaging genetics and their applications in brain MRI, cardiac MRI, and retinal imaging. Early studies suggest that these data-driven approaches can complement traditional IDPs and may expand the phenotypic space available for discovery of heritable imaging traits, although broader validation across cohorts, ancestries, scanners, and imaging protocols remains needed.

selected_papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a frequent complication of heart failure (HF), markedly increasing morbidity and mortality. Although atrial fibrosis is increasingly recognized as a central mechanistic substrate linking HF to AF, the molecular determinants driving fibrotic remodeling and enabling early AF discrimination in HF remain poorly defined. METHODS: We integrated label-free quantitative plasma proteomics with machine learning-based feature selection to analyze samples from 59 age- and sex-matched patients hospitalized with acute decompensated HF. Differentially expressed proteins were subjected to functional and pathway enrichment analyses, and candidate biomarkers were prioritized using an incremental feature selection framework. AHNAK, the top-ranked candidate, was functionally interrogated in vitro using TGF-β1-stimulated primary mouse atrial fibroblasts with siRNA-mediated knockdown and in vivo using a pressure overload-induced HF model in AHNAK heterozygous mice. A two-sample Mendelian randomization analysis was performed to evaluate the association between genetically proxied AHNAK expression and AF risk. RESULTS: Plasma proteomic profiling identified 126 proteins that were significantly dysregulated in HF patients with AF compared with those in sinus rhythm, among which AHNAK was the most upregulated. Machine learning-based feature selection consistently ranked AHNAK as the most discriminative protein, with robust performance for AF discrimination in HF patients (AUC = 0.897, 95% confidence interval: 0.82-0.97). Functionally, AHNAK heterozygous deficiency promoted a profibrotic phenotype, characterized by increased expression of α-smooth muscle actin, fibronectin, and collagen Iα in atrial fibroblasts and exacerbated atrial fibrosis and cardiac dysfunction in pressure-overloaded mice. Mendelian randomization analysis demonstrated a significant protective effect of higher AHNAK expression against AF, with no evidence of horizontal pleiotropy. CONCLUSIONS: This study identifies AHNAK as a discriminative plasma biomarker for AF in HF patients and implicates AHNAK deficiency as a contributor to atrial fibrotic remodeling and AF pathogenesis. External validation in larger and prospective HF cohorts will be required to confirm the clinical utility of AHNAK for AF risk stratification and early detection.

selected_papers.abstract_full: OBJECTIVE: To identify factors associated with predischarge morbidity and mortality among small for gestational age infants. STUDY DESIGN: We conducted a retrospective single-center cohort study of small for gestational age infants admitted to a level IV neonatal intensive care unit. We determined the association of clinical characteristics, congenital anomalies, and genetic disorders with the primary outcome of predischarge morbidity or mortality and characterized morbidity and mortality across congenital anomaly subgroups. RESULTS: Among 293 small for gestational age infants, 18 (6.1%) had a genetic disorder and 103 (35.2%) had a major congenital anomaly, with congenital heart disease (CHD) representing the largest subgroup. The primary outcome of morbidity or mortality occurred in 93 infants (31.7%); 74 infants (25.3%) experienced morbidity and 19 (6.5%) died. CHD (adjusted odds ratio [aOR]: 16.5, 95% CI 6.44-45.7) and multiple congenital anomalies (aOR: 17.8, 95% CI 4.64-71.1) were found to be strongly associated with morbidity or mortality, after accounting for sex, maternal race, and intubation > 7 days. Statistically significant associations were also found with the presence of musculoskeletal anomalies as well as genetic disorders in infants without congenital anomalies, though in limited sample sizes. CHD was the largest contributor to morbidity, whereas multiple congenital anomalies accounted for the greatest proportion of mortality. Infants with abdominal wall defects and central nervous system anomalies experienced no morbidity or mortality. CONCLUSION: Congenital heart disease and multiple congenital anomalies were strongly associated with morbidity and mortality among SGA infants, whereas the degree of SGA alone was not. These findings suggest that risk is not explained by the degree of SGA alone and may be more strongly associated with congenital disease and other underlying factors. KEY POINTS: Risk is highly variable in SGA infantsCHD predicts adverse outcomesMultiple anomalies predict adverse outcomesDegree of SGA alone does not explain risk.

selected_papers.abstract_full: During development, collective and oriented cell behaviors that drive organ formation and tissue patterning require coordination among neighboring cells governed by the highly conserved planar cell polarity (PCP) pathway. Deficiencies in PCP gene function result in severe developmental defects in model systems from flies to mice, while PCP gene mutations are associated with human birth defects impacting the neural tube and heart. Atypical cadherin Celsr1 engages in cell-cell adhesion to coordinate the asymmetric localization of Fz6 and Vangl2 to opposing sides of the PCP junction between neighboring cells. However, whether CELSR1 genetic variations disrupt function or contribute to disease pathogenesis remains poorly understood. Using cell-based assays for Celsr1 function, along with in silico modeling, we test a cohort of 17 Celsr1 mutations previously identified in patients with neural tube and congenital heart defects. In junctional enrichment assays, we find 13 variants displayed altered enrichment at cell borders relative to WT, including both loss- and gain-of-function behaviors. Further analysis of select Celsr1 mutations revealed defects in membrane mobility and perturbed co-recruitment of PCP protein Fz6. Our findings link Celsr1 mutations associated with human birth defects to functional defects in adhesion and PCP. In addition, our approach supports a framework for evaluating PCP function alongside genomics and in silico predictions toward understanding the pathophysiology impacts of genetic variations associated with human developmental disorders and gaining insight into Celsr1 function during development.

selected_papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Kleefstra syndrome type 1 (KLEFS1) is a rare neurodevelopmental disorder caused by pathogenic variants in EHMT1, which play a key role in epigenetic regulation. Core features include global developmental delay (GDD), intellectual disability (ID), facial dysmorphism, congenital heart defects (CHDs), and neuropsychiatric manifestations. METHODS: This retrospective study included patients with KLEFS1 evaluated at Seoul National University Hospital between January 2022 and April 2025. Genetic diagnoses were made using chromosomal microarray or whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing, and clinical data were extracted from medical records. To enhance statistical power, we conducted a joint analysis with established cohorts of at least 30 clinically characterized patients. RESULTS: Among the 15 patients with KLEFS1, 14 (93.3%) exhibited GDD or ID, with frequent comorbidities such as CHDs (8/12, 66.7%), orthopaedic manifestations (6/12, 50.0%), epilepsy (6/15, 40.0%), and sleep problems (4/11, 36.4%). Brain MRI revealed abnormalities in 10 of the 12 patients (83.3%), including pituitary anomalies in 2 (16.7%). By combining our data with recently published multicenter international cohorts, we assessed genotype-phenotype correlations by comparing the clinical features of 202 patients with different variant subtypes. Patients with multigene deletions had a significantly higher prevalence of CHDs (53.5% vs 25.8%, p value = 2 × 10-4), cortical visual impairment (12.5% vs 1.7%, p value = 0.004), microcephaly (37.1% vs 17.8%, p value = 0.009), corpus callosum abnormalities (17.9% vs 5.9%, p value = 0.02), and hearing impairment (39.7% vs 25.6%, p value = 0.04) than those with single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) or short insertions/deletions (indels), in addition to the previously identified features including epilepsy, constipation, and short stature. We also observed that a recurrent EHMT1 variant (p.Arg948Trp), identified in multiple unrelated patients, was linked to significant phenotypic heterogeneity, including late-onset neurocognitive regression. DISCUSSION: Our study showed that patients with multigene deletions are significantly more likely to exhibit multiorgan involvement, including CHDs, cortical visual impairments, microcephaly, corpus callosum abnormalities, and hearing impairments, compared with those with SNVs or indels, emphasizing the importance of genotype-informed management. We report pituitary gland abnormalities in KLEFS1, expanding the phenotypic and neuroimaging spectrum of KLEFS1. The patient showing regression in their 30s necessitates long-term, comprehensive studies to support care.

selected_papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: Cardiomyopathy with a restrictive phenotype is uncommon, genetically heterogeneous, and difficult to distinguish from advanced hypertrophic or dilated cardiomyopathy. We aimed primarily to determine the diagnostic yield and spectrum of pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants among patients with an echocardiographically defined restrictive phenotype; genotype-imaging and survival comparisons were prespecified exploratory analyses. METHODS: We screened 568 patients with cardiomyopathy who underwent whole-exome sequencing and comprehensive echocardiography. Thirty-three met the operational definition of restrictive phenotype. Variants were classified. Genotype-imaging associations and survival were analyzed exploratorily. RESULTS: Among the 568 patients, 33 exhibited a restrictive phenotype: 7 had restrictive cardiomyopathy (RCM), 20 had hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with a restrictive phenotype (HRCM), and 6 had dilated cardiomyopathy with a restrictive phenotype (HDRCM). Variant carriers had a smaller aortic sinus diameter. In addition, MYBPC3 variant carriers had greater ventricular wall thickness and more frequent septal hypertrophy. Both the HRCM and HDRCM groups showed hypertrophic features, with interventricular septal hypertrophy occurring more frequently in the HDRCM group. The estimated 5-year survival was 54.5%, and survival did not differ significantly according to genetic-variant status. CONCLUSIONS: Pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants were frequent in this single-center cohort with restrictive physiology and were associated with selected imaging features. These exploratory findings support integrated genetic and echocardiographic evaluation.

selected_papers.abstract_full: Truncating variants in the TTN gene (TTNtv) are the most common genetic causes of dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM). Despite this high prevalence, the clinical spectrum of TTNtv-associated cardiomyopathy remains incompletely characterized, with variable penetrance, expressivity, and phenotypic manifestations. In this study, we present four cases of TTNtv cardiomyopathy illustrating diverse clinical presentations: an asymptomatic phenotype with moderate left ventricular systolic dysfunction discovered through screening, a severe arrhythmic phenotype with ventricular tachycardia storm requiring multiple ablations and implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) shocks, a recurrent stress-induced (takotsubo) presentation with two discrete episodes, which we present as a hypothesis-generating observation, and an inflammatory presentation with fluorodeoxyglucose-positron emission tomography (FDG-PET) evidence of active myocardial inflammation and symptomatic response to corticosteroids. These cases illustrate the potential clinical value of genetic testing, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, and individualized assessment in TTNtv cardiomyopathy, and suggest that genetic counseling and cascade testing should be considered for affected individuals and their families.

selected_papers.abstract_full: Mutations in β-cardiac myosin are a common cause of inherited cardiomyopathies. The dilated cardiomyopathy E525K mutation alters both thick filament regulation and motor activity, yet the structural basis for these effects has remained unclear. Here, we combined cryo-EM and MD simulations to determine how E525K affects the conformational landscape of cardiac myosin in both its autoinhibited interacting-heads motif (IHM) and isolated myosin head states. E525K-mutated myosin exclusively adopted a single S2 conformation in IHM, in contrast to the conformational heterogeneity observed in wild-type myosin. Structural and electrostatic analyses revealed that the mutation increased positive charge density at the blocked-head (BH) - S2 (subfragment-2) interface, strengthening interactions with negatively charged residues within S2. 3D variability analysis and MD simulations of the E525K IHM demonstrated reduced S2 mobility, consistent with strengthened BH - S2 interactions, and decreased conformational flexibility, providing a structural mechanism for stabilization of the IHM state. To investigate the isolated myosin head, we determined cryo-EM structures of wild-type and E525K subfragment-1 (S1). The mutation induced local conformational rearrangements in the activation-loop and Loop 3 region, the SH3-like domain, and the essential light chain of S1, revealing structural changes that support the enhanced motor activity previously reported for isolated E525K myosin motors. These findings show that E525K stabilizes the autoinhibited IHM through electrostatic stabilization of the BH - S2 interface while inducing structural changes consistent with activation of the isolated motor domain, providing structural insights into how a single DCM mutation differentially regulates cardiac myosin S1 and IHM structure and function.

selected_papers.abstract_full: PURPOSE: Pathogenic variants in CDH2 cause agenesis of the corpus callosum, cardiac, ocular, and genital syndrome (ACOGS). We aimed to define the clinical and molecular landscape of CDH2-related developmental disorders. METHODS: Newly identified and previously reported families were analyzed for genotype-phenotype correlations; variants were assessed using protein modeling and splicing assays. RESULTS: Screening identified 20 new families carrying (likely) pathogenic ((L)P) alleles (n=16) or high-priority variants of uncertain significance (VUS) (n=4), including 12 novel CDH2 alleles. The combined (L)P cohort (37 individuals) showed variable ACOGS core features (mean 3; range 1-5), along with abdominal wall and/or diaphragmatic hernias and nipple, spine or gastrointestinal anomalies, each seen in ∼20% of individuals. Novel ACOGS findings included ambiguous genitalia, female genital malformations and dilated cardiomyopathy. Missense variants, principally within extracellular cadherin domains, accounted for 86% of unique (L)P alleles with clusters in EC1 and EC4-EC5; the remainder produce late protein truncations or in-frame deletions. Disruption of calcium binding was predicted by modeling. Conversely, VUS were primarily nonsense-mediated decay-sensitive or deletions (71%), linked to neurodevelopmental, kidney or other anomalies. CONCLUSION: We expand the ACOGS spectrum and highlight its striking clinical variability. Additionally, we identify a possible milder phenotype associated with CDH2 haploinsufficiency.
